title: 'Finally an Indian I'd vote for':  Ann Coulter, who once said she would never vote for Vivek Ramaswamy because he is of Indian origin, now supports Saritha Komatireddy
text: Ann Coulter who said she would never vote for Vivek Ramaswamy because of his Indian origin says she supports Saritha Komatireddy. Conservative commentator Ann Coulter has publicly expressed support for Indian-American Republican candidate Saritha Komatireddy in the New York attorney general race, saying she wants to vote for her while questioning why she is polling at just 5%. "Finally an Indian I'd vote for and SHE'S AT 5%??? What kind of country is this?" Coulter wrote in a post on X (formerly Twitter) on November 2, reacting to the betting odds for the New York attorney general election. Watch WATCH: Vivek Ramaswamy Nearly Drops Military Kid At Trumpâs Ohio Rally; Then Nasty Kamala Dig Komatireddy is the Republican and Conservative Party candidate challenging incumbent Democratic Attorney General Letitia James in the November 3 midterm elections. Coulter's remarks have attracted attention because of her previous comments about another Indian-American Republican politician, Vivek Ramaswamy. During an appearance on Ramaswamy's podcast in May 2024, Coulter told him she would not have voted for him in the presidential election because he was Indian. "I still would not have voted for you, because you're an Indian," she told Ramaswamy. The former Republican presidential candidate later acknowledged her remarks in a post on X, saying Coulter had told him directly that she could not vote for him because he was Indian, even though she agreed with him on several issues. Coulter's latest comment about Komatireddy has therefore drawn attention as she publicly expressed a willingness to vote for an Indian-American candidate. Who is Saritha Komatireddy? Saritha Komatireddy is a former federal prosecutor, a lecturer at Columbia Law School and a former chief of staff of the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA). She served as an assistant US attorney in the Eastern District of New York, where she held several leadership positions involving national security, cybercrime, narcotics and money laundering cases. She also served as the DEA's chief of staff from 2023 to 2024. A Harvard College and Harvard Law School graduate, Komatireddy was also nominated by President Donald Trump in 2020 to serve as a federal judge in the Eastern District of New York. Her nomination was not confirmed by the Senate. She is now a partner at the law firm Holtzman Vogel and teaches at Columbia Law School. Komatireddy is challenging Letitia James, who has served as New York attorney general since 2019. What is Komatireddy promising? Public safety is a central theme of Komatireddy's campaign. She has called for tougher action against repeat offenders, changes to New York's bail policies and stronger prosecution of crime. She has also made government fraud and corruption investigations part of her campaign platform. In interviews, Komatireddy has criticised James's approach to public safety and argued that the attorney general's office should do more to tackle crime and fraud. Why did Coulter mention the 5% figure? Coulter's post referred to betting-market odds for the New York attorney general contest. A market-tracking report on November 2 put Komatireddy at around 5%, compared with approximately 95% for James. The figures represent market-implied probabilities, not the percentage of voters supporting either candidate. They should not be confused with opinion-poll results. New Yorkers will vote on November 3 to decide whether James will secure another term or be replaced by Komatireddy. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

title: 1 in 4 South Asian Americans who backed Trump in 2024 now plan to vote Democrat in midterms: Survey
text: Trump may be losing some South Asian voters ahead of US midterms At least 25% of South Asian Americans who voted for US President Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election plan to back Democratic candidates in the November 3 midterm elections, according to a survey by advocacy group Indian American Impact. The survey identified the cost of living (65%), healthcare (53%), jobs and wages (33%), and education (28%) as the key issues influencing voters ahead of the midterms. Watch 'Veto, Veto, Veto...': Trump Hints At Massive 'Unrest' If Democrats Win Midterms Of the 800 registered South Asian voters surveyed, 87% were Indian-Americans, while the remaining 13% were from Pakistani, Bangladeshi, Sri Lankan, Nepali, Bhutanese, Maldivian, Afghani, Khmer and Burmese communities. Among respondents who voted for Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election, 96% said they planned to vote for a Democratic candidate in the upcoming polls. The survey found that while 67% of South Asian Americans who voted for Trump continued to support Republicans, 25% planned to vote for Democrats. The findings come as early voting has begun in several states, including Texas, where Democratic nominee James Talarico is locked in a tight race against Republican Ken Paxton, who has Trump's backing. Vasant Bhatt, a 21-year-old second-generation Indian-American who interned on Senator Ted Cruz's election campaign in 2024, said in a social media post that he had voted for Talarico. "I just cast my ballot for James Talarico. As a second-generation Indian American, I am thoroughly disgusted by the xenophobia, racial resentment, and increasingly brazen attacks on my identity," Bhatt wrote. The survey also pointed to widespread concerns about discrimination. As many as 90% of registered voters said they had experienced discrimination or knew someone who had, while 48% said they had personally faced it. âIt comes as no surprise that a quarter of Trumpâs 2024 voters in our community plan to vote Democratic. This community can make the margin, and we are working to reach every voter who can,â Chintan Patel, executive director of Indian American Impact, said in a statement. The survey found that 16% of respondents had not voted in any general election since 2020. It also highlighted a broader sense of disillusionment with elected representatives. While 78% of respondents believed their vote could bring about change, 79% felt elected officials quickly lost touch with ordinary people. Another 67% said public officials did not care about the views of people like them, while 43% felt they had no say in government decisions. The findings underscore the potential electoral influence of South Asian American voters, particularly in closely contested states. Michigan has around 187,000 South Asian residents. Nearly 30,000 registered South Asian voters did not vote in 2022, exceeding the roughly 19,000-vote margin that decided the state's 2024 Senate race. Texas, meanwhile, has more than 700,000 South Asian residents, with nearly 100,000 registered South Asian voters having sat out the 2022 elections. The Indian-American community also has a significant presence in California, Texas, New Jersey, New York, Washington, Illinois, Pennsylvania and Georgia. In battleground states such as Georgia, Pennsylvania, Michigan and North Carolina, where electoral contests can be decided by narrow margins, even a shift of one or two percentage points in voter support could influence the outcome. title: US charges 48 non-citizens over election-related crimes in Pennsylvania, California, Florida, New York and Nevada; two Indians among those accused of illegal voting and false citizenship claims
text: US Justice Department announces charges against 48 non-citizens in election-related cases across five states. (Photo: Office of Public Affairs) The US Department of Justice has announced charges against 48 non-US citizens in connection with alleged election-related offences across several states, including Pennsylvania, California, Florida, New York and Nevada. The cases involve allegations of illegal voting in federal elections, fraudulent voter registration and falsely claiming US citizenship to register or cast ballots. In a press release issued on October 26, 2026, the department detailed cases filed across multiple federal judicial districts. Several defendants are also accused of making false statements during naturalisation proceedings, including allegedly concealing previous voter registration or voting activity. The department said the cases involve both misdemeanour and felony charges, depending on the alleged offences. Two Indian nationals among those charged Two Indian nationals have been named in the announcement. Amandeep Kaur, 30, a lawful permanent resident who is seeking US citizenship, has been accused of registering to vote in December 2022 and voting in the November 2024 US election. The case has been filed in the Central District of California. Watch BREAKING: Horror BLOODBATH In Pennsylvania; Children, Pregnant Women Killed In Mass Shooting Kamlesh Navnitlal Shah, 67, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged in the Eastern District of California with voting by a non-citizen. According to the Justice Department, Shah allegedly registered to vote on the day of the November 2024 general election and cast a ballot that day. He has been charged by information. Both individuals face allegations that have yet to be proven in court. Pennsylvania cases involve nine defendants In Pennsylvania, nine non-citizens have been charged across two federal judicial districts with allegedly voting in elections involving federal offices. In the Eastern District, the defendants include Alfredo Santiesteban, 73, a Cuban national described as an illegal alien; Artur Kopacz, 50, a Polish national; Osmal Loy, 70, a Cuban national; and Yehuda Peer, 30, an Israeli national. The latter three are identified as lawful permanent residents. Prosecutors allege that the four voted in the 2022 or 2024 general elections. In the Middle District, the defendants include Kenyan nationals Nina Nyawara, 21, and Joyce Donovan, 38; Russian national Inna Henry, 52; Dutch national Joyce Pitts, 80; and Greek national Nourten Kuruju, 64. All are described as lawful permanent residents. The allegations concern voting in federal elections held in 2022 or 2024. California cases include allegations of voter fraud and naturalisation fraud The cases involve alleged voter registration fraud and false claims of US citizenship. (Photo: Office of Public Affairs) California accounts for several of the cases detailed by the department, with allegations ranging from illegal voting to false statements in citizenship applications. In the Central District of California, 13 defendants face felony charges, including allegations involving naturalisation applications. They include Belizean national Omar Alexander Munoz, 72, who allegedly registered to vote in 2019 while claiming to be a US citizen and voted in elections in 2020, twice in 2022 and in 2024. He is also accused of making a false statement in his naturalisation application. Other defendants in the district include Salvadoran national Ana Dominguez, 60; Guatemalan national Axel Giovani Prera Garcia, 46; Mexican nationals Flavio Alejandro Zuniga, 43, Ernest Gutierrez Ruvalcaba, 57, Jesus Narez-Madrigal, 52, Jose Antonio Banuelos-Diaz, 42, and Sulema de Leon, 35; Cambodian national Butleng Taing, 43; Honduran national Carlos Antonio Galeas, 54; Pakistani national Muhammad Khan, 50; and Canadian national Rouzbeh Seyamaknejad, 63. The allegations vary and include fraudulent registration, illegal voting and false statements in naturalisation paperwork. In the Eastern District of California, six defendants have been charged with voting by a non-citizen in a federal election. They include Mexican nationals Maricela Nazarin Gonzalez, 43, Camino Giles Jimenez, 51, and Juan Antonio Rivas Garcia, 46; Guatemalan national Rony de Jesus Sicaja, 38; Filipino national Giezell Viduya Adawag, 41; and Indian national Kamlesh Navnitlal Shah, 67. The Justice Department said the offence of voting by a non-citizen in a federal election carries a statutory maximum sentence of one year in federal prison. In the Northern District of California, five defendants face allegations involving illegal voting and false statements during naturalisation proceedings. They are Mexican national Veronica Bullene, 43; Georgian national David Shapiro, 41; Myanmar national Moe Thida Lwin, 57; Tongan national Manakotau Mataele Finau, 61; and Ecuadoran national Maribel del Carmen Garces Barriga, 62. The Southern District of California has four defendants facing allegations of falsely claiming US citizenship to vote, unlawful attempts to obtain naturalisation and false statements under oath. They include Filipino nationals Jose Probitsado Amaro, 51, and Pamele Arbues Line, 56; Canadian national Jennifer Jung, 31; and Guatemalan national Erick Ronaldo Soto Mendizabal, 64. Six defendants charged in Florida In the Middle District of Florida, six defendants have been charged with election-related offences. They include Cuban nationals Jamie Orlando Sosa Sardina, 60, and Luis Manuel Perez, 72; Ecuadorian national Martha Haydee Desantis, 81; Canadian nationals Lise Marie Johnson, 69, and Diane Wendy Curley, 55; and Brazilian national Pedro Igor A. Franco, 37. According to the department, Sardina, Desantis and Johnson face allegations of falsely claiming US citizenship to vote and voting illegally. The remaining defendants have been accused of voting by non-citizens. The alleged conduct includes voting in the 2022 and 2024 federal general elections. New York and Nevada cases In New York, German national Marva Cook, 66, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged in the Northern District with voting by a non-citizen. In the Eastern District of New York, three lawful permanent residents - Irish national Eoin Cranney, 35; Guyanese national Ronald Sheldon Baird, 47; and Jamaican national Karlene Daniels Samuels, 55 - have been charged with voting by non-citizens in federal elections. Prosecutors allege that all three submitted fraudulent voter registration applications and voted in the 2024 general election. The department also said the defendants made admissions about their non-citizen status and voting activity during voluntary interviews with federal agents. In Nevada, Filipino national Jullie Ann Sumalinog Moore, 44, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with voting by a non-citizen in an election involving federal offices, including the presidency and seats in Congress. Charges do not establish guilt The cases involve allegations of illegal voting, fraudulent voter registration, false claims of US citizenship and misrepresentations in naturalisation proceedings. The charges differ according to the conduct prosecutors allege in each case. The Justice Department clarified that complaints, indictments and information contain allegations rather than findings of guilt. All defendants are presumed innocent unless and until they are proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in court. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

title: Pope Leo XIV casts ballot in US midterms, becomes first pontiff to vote in a US general election
text: Pope Leo XIV/Image: AP Pope Leo XIV has voted in the 2026 US midterm elections, becoming the first sitting pope to cast a ballot in a US general election, the Vatican confirmed on Friday. The Chicago-born pontiff submitted a mail-in ballot in his home state of Illinois ahead of the November elections. The Holy See press office said Leo, formerly known as Robert Prevost, had exercised his voting rights whenever he was eligible as a US citizen. "The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes," the Vatican statement said. The confirmation followed a report by the Chicago Sun-Times, which cited the chief of staff at the Will County clerk's office as saying that Leo had requested a mail-in ballot on October 3. He is registered at an address in New Lenox, Illinois. It remains unclear how the pontiff returned his ballot. His brother, John Prevost, was in Rome this week accompanying parishioners from St Jude's, an Augustinian-run church in New Lenox where the pope attends Mass. Leo also addressed the parish in 2024, when he was still a cardinal. The Vatican said Leo had also voted while living in Peru whenever he was eligible. His participation in the US midterms reflects his stated belief that citizens should take part in democratic elections. Records from the Illinois State Board of Elections cited by the AP show that Prevost requested ballots in five primary elections since 2000. He selected Democratic ballots in 2008 and 2010, followed by Republican ballots in 2012, 2014 and 2016. Illinois voters must declare a party preference when requesting a ballot in a primary election, which determines each party's candidates for the general election. However, voters are not required to declare a party preference when voting in general elections. The records also show that Prevost submitted ballots in every US general election since 2000 except those held in 2020 and 2022. They do not identify which candidates he supported in any election. His voting history spans two Illinois counties. While registered in Cook County, which is heavily Democratic, he requested Democratic primary ballots. After moving to Will County, a more conservative suburban area, he selected Republican ballots in three consecutive primary elections. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. title: GVMC records 56.3% turnout, with core city areas lagging behind peripheral zones in voter participation
text: Visakhapatnam : The Greater Visakhapatnam Municipal Corporation (GVMC) election recorded a voter turnout of 56.32%, significantly lower than the 59.41% polled in 2021 and the 64% to 80% recorded across assembly constituencies within GVMC limits in the 2024 general elections. The turnout, nearly 15 percentage points below the 2024 assembly election levels in some areas, has triggered speculation among political parties over its possible impact on the results, which will be declared on Tuesday. While low polling has been a recurring feature of municipal elections in Visakhapatnam, parties had expected a better response, given growing political awareness and increased access to information through technology. The core city areas once again recorded lower polling than the peripheral zones, following a pattern similar to the 2024 assembly elections. Zone-wise turnout ranged from 49.71% to 66.27%. Bheemili topped the list with 66.27%, followed by Anakapalli (65.6%), Aganampudi (62.08%) and Gajuwaka (60.9%). West zone recorded 58.97%, while Pendurthi and Madhurawada registered 55.12% and 55.07%, respectively. East and South zones polled 54.21% and 52.61%, respectively. North zone recorded the lowest turnout at 49.71%. A similar pattern was evident in the 2024 assembly elections, when the four core city constituencies recorded relatively low polling. Vizag South registered 63.42%, the lowest, followed by North (64.63%), East (68.5%) and West (69.78%). All four constituencies fell short of the stateâs overall assembly election turnout of 80.66%. Among the seven assembly constituencies in Visakhapatnam district, only Pendurthi and Bheemili crossed the 70% mark, recording 74% and 76%, respectively. Anakapalli registered nearly 80%. The subdued turnout has left both major political parties assessing its possible implications for the mayoral contest and corporator results. The TDP is confident of securing the mayorâs post and a majority of the corporator seats. The YSRCP, meanwhile, is banking on cross-voting to win the mayoral election, while hoping to secure 40 to 50 of the 120 corporator seats. YSRCP leaders believe the candidature of MLC and party state womenâs wing president Varudu Kalyani has helped the party attract urban, educated voters and professionals. They expect this support to translate into a narrow victory in the mayoral contest. The TDP, on the other hand, is banking on its mayoral candidate, young corporator Mukka Sravani, arguing that her five years of work among the public will give the party an advantage. Political analysts attribute the low turnout to a combination of urban voter apathy, lacklustre campaigning and the absence of a strong political wave or compelling local issues. The delayed finalisation of candidates and release of manifestos also left parties with limited time to reach out to voters. Cyclone Arnab further disrupted normal life and electioneering during the crucial final days of campaigning, potentially affecting voter mobilisation. Another factor cited by observers is the cityâs growing migrant population. Many of those who have moved to Visakhapatnam in recent years may not yet have developed strong political connections with local leaders or the same level of engagement with civic affairs as long-time residents. Low-key contests in several wards and inadequate voter outreach may have further contributed to the subdued response. title: 'Won't forgive and forget': Rahul Gandhi at 'CEC impeachment' event - top quotes
text: NEW DELHI: Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi on Saturday said that the Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar should not only be impeached but also prosecuted for treason over the alleged irregularities in Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls. In his closing remarks during the mock parliament of INDIA bloc, Rahul said that the opposition has enough proof to make sure that Gyanesh Kumar cannot survive as the Chief Election Commissioner. Watch They Want Ruckus, Not Debate: Amit Shahâs Big Challenge To INDIA Bloc Over Vote Theft, CEC, SIR Row Here are the top quotes from Congress leader's address The Election Commission itself is stating that the 2024 Lok Sabha election is an illegal election, and the people who entered the Lok Sabha, the BJP people who entered the Lok Sabha, did so illegally. I just want to make one small point. 13.3 crore voters were deleted. That is one in every seven Indians. 15% of India's voters were deleted. In the last Lok Sabha election, these voters supposedly voted. The difference between the opposition and those who won the election was a 3% vote margin. So, the election was won by a 3% vote, and now the Election Commission itself is saying that 15% of those voters should never have voted. Which means that the Election Commission itself is stating that the 2024 Lok Sabha election is an illegal election, and the people who entered the Lok Sabha, the BJP people who entered the Lok Sabha, did so illegally. Mr Gyanesh Kumar is not going to survive as the Chief Election Commissioner. We already have enough proof to make sure that this gentleman cannot survive. And if the BJP insists on keeping him after we reveal what we know, then it will be very clear what the BJP's game is. This looks like a meeting of Lok Sabha MPs, Rajya Sabha MPs, and common citizens. But actually, this is a political weapon . This is an extremely dangerous political weapon that is sitting in the garden of the Leader of the Opposition in the Rajya Sabha, and this weapon is targeted directly at every single person, starting from Mr Gyanesh Kumar, going to Mr Modi, going to Mr Shah, and every single person who has colluded to destroy the vote of the Indian people. Remember, you will not always hide behind that institution. Remember that one day, today or tomorrow, you are going to face the representatives of the people of India. Mr Modi and Mr Shah might be on top. We will deal with them, but you are their instruments, and so you are our first target. So if Mr Gyanesh Kumar thinks, or the five or seven people below him think, that immunity will save them, I would kindly suggest to them, with love and affection, to take a look at what is going on in the country. Please understand the mood of the people outside. You will see tomorrow itself. You will see tomorrow that a political weapon is going to be placed on the streets of Delhi. A united opposition is going to show you exactly what the mood of the people of this country is. You can continue to rig the elections. You can continue to control and allow the misuse of the CBI, the ED, and every single institution of this country. But we guarantee you that this is a temporary phenomenon. title: TOI Bharat Abroad: US midterms - red, blue & a little desi too
text: India has wrapped up its election-season drama for the year, and the spotlight now shifts from the worldâs biggest democracy to the worldâs oldest. It's America's turn to count the votes, count the dollars and count on candidates to make their case. Indian-Americans are in the race, South Asian voters may be rethinking their loyalties, and Elon Musk is spending big. The US midterms are shaping up to be quite a ballot show. So, without further ado, letâs go! THE BIG STORY The desi ballot: From Capitol Hill to cowboy country The countdown to November 3 is on, and Indian-American candidates are fighting for a bigger place in the American political landscape. Some are defending seats they already hold, others are chasing their first election victory, and a handful are aiming for positions that could take them well beyond Congress. The big picture Four Indian-origin Democrats, Ro Khanna, Pramila Jayapal, Ami Bera and Suhas Subramanyam, are seeking re-election to the US House of Representatives. Republican Vivek Ramaswamy is running for governor of Ohio, while physician-turned-politician Amish Shah is trying to win an open congressional seat in Arizona. The field extends well beyond these familiar names. Pia Dandiya is contesting Florida's 22nd Congressional District, Republican Saritha Komatireddy is challenging New York Attorney General Letitia James, and Indian-origin candidates are competing for state-level offices across the country. Two House contests offer a particularly unusual twist: Indian-origin candidates are facing one another from opposing parties. In California's 17th Congressional District, Khanna faces Republican Ritesh Tandon. In Washington's 7th District, Jayapal is defending her seat against Republican Nirav Sheth. The Ohio governor's race is drawing national attention. Polling snapshots show a contest between Ramaswamy and Democratic candidate Amy Acton, a physician and former state health official. A RealClearPolling average dated October 19 put Acton at 48.7% and Ramaswamy at 44.3%, while a Fox News poll conducted from October 15 to 19 showed a narrower 50%-48% margin. The difference between the polls is a reminder that surveys are snapshots, not verdicts. Why it matters The midterms will decide control of Congress for the final two years of Donald Trump's presidency. All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are being contested, alongside gubernatorial and other state-level races. A change in congressional control could reshape the administration's legislative prospects and its ability to secure support for its policies. For Indian-Americans, the stakes go beyond the fate of individual candidates. Their growing presence in public office is bringing the community into debates on immigration, technology, healthcare, jobs, housing and US foreign policy, including relations with India. But there is no single Indian-American political agenda. The candidates span the ideological spectrum and offer sharply different ideas about government, immigration and the economy. Their electoral fortunes will depend on their own campaigns, local concerns and the national political climate, not simply on their heritage. The results will provide a measure of how far Indian-origin candidates have progressed from being a relatively small presence in American politics to competing for influence across Congress, state legislatures and governors' offices. The question is whether that growing visibility can translate into more seats and greater political influence. A new survey suggests that a portion of those voters are considering a different choice in the November 3 midterms. The survey by advocacy group Indian American Impact found that at least 25% of South Asian Americans who voted for Trump in the 2024 presidential election now intend to support Democratic candidates. The findings are based on 800 registered South Asian voters, 87% of whom were Indian-American. The issues weighing on respondents include the cost of living, cited by 65%, healthcare at 53%, jobs and wages at 33%, and education at 28%. The survey also found that 67% of South Asian respondents who voted for Trump in 2024 still planned to back Republican candidates, underlining that the community's preferences remain mixed. The numbers offer a snapshot, not a prediction of how the entire community will vote. Nor do they establish that every respondent who plans to change their vote will do so on polling day. Still, the findings suggest that economic pressures, immigration and perceptions of discrimination could influence voting decisions. With several races expected to be closely fought, the question is whether these stated intentions translate into turnout and make a difference at the ballot box. Read full story OFFBEAT The money race: Musk's $445 million midterm bet Campaigns run on candidates and their messages, but the American midterms also come with an eye-watering price tag. Elon Musk has contributed more than $445 million to political groups during the current election cycle, emerging as one of the biggest donors to political action committees in US history, according to a report. Federal Election Commission filings show that Musk contributed $77 million to America PAC in the first two weeks of October. Since relaunching the group in July, he has given it $355 million, averaging $3.6 million a day, Bloomberg reported. The spending comes as both sides pour money into races that could determine control of Congress. Through October 14, Republican committees, congressional super PACs and Trump's MAGA Inc. had raised a combined $2.1 billion, compared with $1.4 billion raised by corresponding Democratic committees, according to the report. The figures illustrate how wealthy donors and outside political groups have become major forces in American campaigning. Their money can fund advertising, voter outreach and efforts to shape the debate, although donations alone cannot determine how people vote. Musk's involvement also puts the spotlight on the wider question of political influence: how much sway can a wealthy individual exercise over an election, and how does that spending translate into votes? The answer will not come from the fundraising totals alone. With polling day approaching, the final results will show how money, candidate appeal, local issues and turnout combine at the ballot box. title: Indian-American Texas student says he's 'politically homeless' after facing backlash for voting for Democrat: 'My biggest concern is....'
text: 21-year-old Indian-American Vasant Bhatt says his future votes are likely to be for the Democrats. 21-year-old Vasant Bhatt announced on social media that despite identifying with conservative politics so far, he voted for Democrat James Talarico in the Texas election against Republican candidate Ken Paxton to reject anti-India hatred in his state and in the US. Though he is a second-generation Indian-American, he was asked to leave the US after his post went viral. The Political Science student of the University of Houston was removed from Campus Reform's correspondent program as an apparent fallout but he said he won't retract his beliefs and neither would he abandon his community. MAGA had a problem with Bhatt putting Indian first in his hyphenated Indian-American identity and still considering Indian-American as his community. In an interview with the Houston Chronicle, he said the social media reactions to his post were disturbing but not shocking. He interned for Republican senator Ted Cruz's 2024 campaign but now he considers himself as "politically homeless", but his future votes would probably go to the Democrats. Rising India hatred driving Indian-Americans to Democrats The original post that Bhatt made was a request to every Indian-American with voting rights to go out and reject the anti-India hatred. "As a second-generation Indian American, I am thoroughly disgusted by the xenophobia, racial resentment, and increasingly brazen attacks on my identity. My family has contributed to the American story through hard work, sacrifice, and an unwavering belief in the opportunities this nation promises. I am every bit as American as anyone else, and I will not tolerate being treated as a perpetual foreigner in the country I call home," Bhatt wrote. "I implore every eligible Texan to get out and vote. This election is about the kind of state and country we are prepared to defendâand the principles we refuse to surrender." Indian Americans historically favored Democrats, but the community sided with Trump in 2024. title: Indian-American candidates in 2026 US midterms: Key races, profiles, latest polling & what's at stake
text: From left: Ami Bera, Pramila Jayapal, Ro Khanna, Suhas Subramanyam and Vivek Ramaswamy. The 2026 US midterm elections are shaping up to be a significant test of Indian-American political representation. Four Indian-origin Democrats â Ro Khanna, Pramila Jayapal, Ami Bera and Suhas Subramanyam â are seeking re-election to the House of Representatives. Meanwhile, Vivek Ramaswamy is locked in a high-octane race for governor of Ohio, and physician-turned-politician Amish Shah is attempting to capture an open Arizona congressional seat. Read also | US midterm elections 2026: Why it's a do-or-die fight for Trump & the Democracts - explained in 10 charts The contests extend beyond Congress. Indian-American candidates are competing for attorney-general positions, mayoralties and seats in state legislatures across the country. The elections on November 3 will take place against the backdrop of a closely divided Congress and a national debate over the economy, immigration, healthcare, technology and Trump's policies. The outcomes could determine not only which party controls Capitol Hill but also how much influence Indian-American lawmakers exercise in Washington and state governments. Indian-Americans in key congressional races 1. Ro Khanna Ro Khanna, one of the most prominent Indian-American Democrats in Congress at the moment, is seeking a sixth term from Californiaâs 17th Congressional District, which covers much of Silicon Valley, including parts of Santa Clara and Alameda counties. He faces Republican Ritesh Tandon in the midterms, after comfortably finishing first in Californiaâs June 2 nonpartisan primary with 62.3% of the vote. Tandon advanced with 14.8%. The district, home to major technology companies and a large population of technology workers, has consistently favoured Democrats. First elected to the House in 2016, Khanna has established himself as a progressive voice on economic policy, technology, foreign affairs and the role of American power overseas. Khanna has been a vocal critic of President Donald Trump, particularly over his economic policies Born in Philadelphia to Indian immigrant parents, he studied economics at the University of Chicago and earned a law degree from Yale University. Before entering Congress, he taught economics at Stanford University, practised law and served as deputy assistant secretary of commerce under President Barack Obama. He now sits on the House Armed Services Committee and has been an influential voice on issues ranging from artificial intelligence and semiconductor manufacturing to US competition with China. Read also | US midterms 2026: Meet Ro Khanna, Indian-American Congressman behind Epstein files push Khanna has been a vocal critic of President Donald Trump, particularly over his economic policies, immigration crackdown and approach to democratic institutions. He has challenged the administrationâs priorities on taxation and economic inequality, arguing that government policy should benefit working families rather than disproportionately favour wealthy individuals and corporations. His opposition to Trump also extends to the presidentâs use of executive power and his approach to foreign policy, where Khanna has advocated greater congressional oversight of military action and a stronger emphasis on diplomacy. At the same time, Khanna has sought to distinguish himself from the Democratic establishment by championing a more populist economic agenda, including investment in manufacturing, clean energy, education and healthcare. His views on technology, economic inequality and Americaâs global role frequently place him at the centre of the partyâs policy debate. 2. Pramila Jayapal Pramila Jayapal is seeking re-election from Washingtonâs 7th Congressional District, which includes much of Seattle and surrounding communities. She faces Republican Nirav Sheth in the midterms after dominating the stateâs nonpartisan primary, securing 84.4% of the vote against Shethâs 9.8%. The result underlined her strong standing in a heavily Democratic district, where she has built a substantial political base through her advocacy on immigration, healthcare and economic inequality. Elected to Congress in 2016, Jayapal made history as the first South Asian American woman elected to the House of Representatives. Pramila Jayapal serves on House committees that give her influence over debates on immigration. Born in India, she moved to the United States at 16 to attend Georgetown University and later earned an MBA from Northwestern University. Before entering electoral politics, she founded OneAmerica, a Washington-based immigrant-rights organisation, and became a prominent campaigner for immigration reform and civil liberties. Her experience as an activist has shaped her legislative priorities, particularly on deportations, detention, family separation and pathways to legal status. Jayapal has championed Medicare for All, stronger labour protections, affordable housing, climate action and expanded access to education. She has also held leadership positions in the Congressional Progressive Caucus and serves on the House Judiciary, Foreign Affairs and Budget committees, giving her influence over debates on immigration enforcement, federal spending and American foreign policy. Read also | US midterms 2026: From immigration reform to $15 minimum wage, all about Pramila Jayapal A vocal critic of President Donald Trump, Jayapal has repeatedly challenged his administrationâs immigration crackdown, deportation policies and restrictions on legal immigration. She has argued that the administrationâs approach threatens civil liberties and undermines protections for immigrant communities. Her opposition also extends to Trumpâs economic agenda and broader use of executive power, with Jayapal advocating stronger social protections and greater accountability for the administration. Her politics frequently put her to the left of the Democratic leadership, although she has worked within the party to advance progressive priorities. 3. Ami Bera Ami Bera, one of the longest-serving Indian-American members of Congress, is seeking another term in Californiaâs 3rd Congressional District, which covers Sacramento County and surrounding communities. He faces Republican Robb Tucker in the November 3 midterm elections. In the stateâs nonpartisan primary, Bera secured 34.3% of the vote against Tucker's 29.9%. His re-election bid comes as Democrats seek to regain control of the House, with the Sacramento region offering a test of whether his established local support can withstand the broader national political climate. Bera has supported stronger US engagement with India. First elected in 2012, Bera has represented the Sacramento area in Congress since January 2013. The son of Indian immigrants, he grew up in California and earned his medical degree from the University of California, Irvine. Before entering politics, he worked as a physician and served as Sacramento Countyâs chief medical officer. His background has helped shape his political identity as a pragmatic Democrat who emphasises healthcare, public services and evidence-based policymaking rather than the more sweeping economic agenda associated with the partyâs progressive wing. Read also | US midterms 2026: Who is Ami Bera, Indian-American Democrat seeking re-election from California's newly redrawn district Healthcare remains a central part of Beraâs political profile. He has advocated improving access to medical care, reducing prescription drug costs and strengthening Medicare, while also focusing on education, infrastructure, veteransâ services and economic development. His approach generally favours targeted reforms and bipartisan cooperation, positioning him closer to the Democratic Partyâs moderate wing on several policy questions. Foreign affairs, however, have become one of his defining areas of influence. Bera has served on the House Foreign Affairs Committee and the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, with a particular interest in the Indo-Pacific. He has supported stronger US engagement with India and closer cooperation with regional partners, while emphasising the strategic challenge posed by China. His work has given him a prominent role in debates over US-India relations, regional security, intelligence oversight and the future of American engagement in Asia. 4. Suhas Subramanyam Suhas Subramanyam is seeking a second term in the US House of Representatives from Virginiaâs 10th Congressional District, which includes Loudoun County and parts of the surrounding Northern Virginia suburbs. He faces Republican Dave Beckwith and independent candidate Ahsen Mujeeb Malik in the midterms. The district, home to technology professionals, federal employees and government contractors, has generally favoured Democrats, but the Trump administrationâs cuts to the federal workforce and changes to government spending have made these issues particularly consequential for local voters. Suhas Subramanyam served as a technology policy adviser in the Obama White House. Subramanyam entered Congress in January 2025 after defeating Republican Mike Clancy in the 2024 election. His victory made him one of the newest Indian-American members of the House. Born in Houston to Indian immigrant parents, he studied at Tulane University and earned a law degree from Northwestern University. Before entering electoral politics, he worked with technology startups and served as a technology policy adviser in the Obama White House. He was elected to Virginiaâs House of Delegates in 2019, becoming the first South Asian American elected to the state legislature, and later served in the Virginia Senate before moving to Congress. His political profile combines technology policy, economic affordability and a focus on practical local concerns. During his time in the Virginia legislature, he worked on issues including utility bills, prescription drug costs, education and gun safety. In Congress, he has emphasised support for small businesses, infrastructure investment, healthcare access and protecting federal workers. His background in technology has also shaped his attention to the rapid expansion of data centres in Northern Virginia, where new developments promise investment and jobs but raise concerns about electricity demand, water consumption, land use and higher infrastructure costs. Read also | US midterms 2026: Meet Suhas Subramanyam, Indian-origin Democrat who served as advisor to Barack Obama Subramanyam has been critical of Trumpâs policies on federal employment and government restructuring, arguing that abrupt cuts and uncertainty can harm public services and communities that depend on government jobs. His district is particularly exposed to such changes because of its concentration of federal agencies, contractors and defence-related businesses. He has also advocated reproductive healthcare protections, stronger gun-safety measures and policies aimed at lowering household expenses. New entrants Amish Shah is running as the Democratic nominee in Arizona's 1st Congressional District. He previously contested the seat in 2024, losing to Republican David Schweikert. Schweikert is now running for governor, leaving the congressional seat open. Shah won the July 21, 2026, Democratic primary with 39.4% of the vote, defeating Marlene GalÃ¡n-Woods, who received 34.4%. He faces Republican Jay Feely, a former NFL kicker, in November. The district is competitive, making this one of the more consequential races involving an Indian-origin congressional candidate. A FirstStrategic poll conducted on October 1 found Shah at 44.4% and Feely at 41.6% among registered voters, with a margin of error of 5.4 percentage points. A forecast updated October 23 projects Shah at 63% to win. Read also | US midterms 2026: Meet Amish Shah, the doctor seeking a second shot at Congress Pia Dandiya is the Democratic nominee in Florida's 22nd Congressional District, an open seat where she faces Republican Casey Askar. Dandiya won the August 18 Democratic primary with 68.6% of the vote, defeating Kaysia Earley. Askar won the Republican primary with 30.9% in a crowded field. Read also | US midterms 2026: Meet Pia Dandiya, Indian-origin Democrat running for Floridaâs open 22nd House seat Ritesh Tandon is the Republican nominee challenging Khanna in California's 17th Congressional District. He advanced through the June 2 top-two primary with 19,793 votes, or 14.8%, finishing behind Khanna. The district is heavily Democratic, and current forecasts show Khanna with a substantial projected advantage. Nirav Sheth is the Republican challenger to Jayapal in Washington's 7th Congressional District. He secured second place in the state's nonpartisan primary, receiving 21,282 votes, or 9.8%. Jayapal won 84.4%. Sheth's advance means the November ballot will feature two races where Indian-origin candidates are facing off from opposing parties. Indian-American politicians not on the ballot Raja Krishnamoorthi lost the Democratic primary for the Illinois Senate seat and will not be the party's nominee in the November Senate election. His absence removes a high-profile Indian-American candidate from one of the year's most prominent Senate contests. Shri Thanedar lost the Democratic primary for Michigan's 13th Congressional District and is not the Democratic nominee in the November race. Gubernatorial race attracting national attention: Vivek Ramaswamy Vivek Ramaswamy, the Indian-American entrepreneur who emerged as a prominent voice in the Republican Party during the 2024 presidential race, is seeking to become governor of Ohio, the state where he was born and raised. The Republican nominee faces Democrat Amy Acton, a physician and former director of the Ohio Department of Health. The contest has become a closely watched test of Ramaswamy's transition from conservative political outsider to candidate for executive office. Born in Cincinnati to Indian immigrant parents, Ramaswamy studied biology at Harvard University and law at Yale. He made his fortune in biotechnology and investment management, founding Roivant Sciences in 2014. His 2021 book, Woke, Inc. , established his political identity as a critic of corporate diversity initiatives, environmental, social and governance investing and what he considers excessive ideological influence over business. Ramaswamy's political relationship with Trump remains a defining feature of his campaign During the 2024 Republican presidential primary, he advocated cutting government bureaucracy, restricting federal spending and challenging established political institutions. Although he withdrew from the race and endorsed Donald Trump, his combative campaign style helped establish him as a nationally recognised conservative figure. Trump subsequently selected Ramaswamy to co-lead the Department of Government Efficiency initiative alongside Elon Musk, although he left before the initiative's major restructuring efforts as he turned to the Ohio governor's race. His gubernatorial platform centres on reducing government costs, deregulation, education reform and expanding economic opportunity. His political relationship with Trump remains a defining feature of his campaign, even as he seeks to establish an independent record as a candidate for state leadership. The campaign has recently been embroiled in controversy over an advertisement featuring Acton's estranged mother criticising her daughter. Read also | US midterms 2026: Meet Vivek Ramaswamy, Trump-backed Republican seeking the Ohio governorship The ad drew bipartisan condemnation, including from DeWine, who urged Ramaswamy to withdraw it. Trump, however, defended the advertisement and encouraged Ramaswamy to continue running it, while Vice-President JD Vance also criticised Republicans who opposed it. The dispute has sharpened questions about the role of personal attacks in the campaign and whether the controversy could affect Ramaswamy's standing with voters. Polling has shown Acton ahead, although the size of her lead varies. The RealClearPolling average for October 19 put Acton at 48.7% and Ramaswamy at 44.3%, while a Fox News poll conducted October 15â19 found a narrower 50-48 margin. Other statewide contests Nirav Shah , a physician and public-health administrator, is the Democratic nominee for governor of Maine. He previously served as director of the Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention from 2019 to 2023 and as principal deputy director of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention from 2023 to 2025. Shah won Maine's June 9 Democratic gubernatorial primary with 26.9% of the vote. Aruna Miller , Maryland's lieutenant governor, is seeking to continue in office on the Democratic ticket led by Governor Wes Moore. Born in India, Miller immigrated to the US as a child and built a career as a transportation engineer before entering politics. Her career includes service in Maryland's House of Delegates and election as lieutenant governor in 2022. Miller's political position differs from that of a standalone gubernatorial candidate: the lieutenant governor runs on a joint ticket with the governor. Her electoral prospects therefore depend on the performance of the ticket as a whole as well as her own profile. Read also | US midterms 2026: Indian-American Democrat Aruna Miller seeks re-election as Maryland Lt Governor alongside Wes Moore Saritha Komatireddy , a Republican lawyer and former federal prosecutor, is the Republican nominee for New York attorney general. She is challenging Democratic incumbent Letitia James. Her campaign offers Republicans an opportunity to contest an office that has become nationally prominent because of high-profile investigations and litigation involving major businesses and political figures. Read also | US midterms 2026: How 9/11 shaped Saritha Komatireddyâs legal career as she runs for New York attorney general Josh Kaul , Wisconsin's Democratic attorney general, is seeking re-election. Nithya Raman: Running for Los Angeles mayor Raman is a Los Angeles City Council member and urban planner seeking to unseat Mayor Karen Bass. Her campaign focuses on housing, homelessness, city services and the cost of living. She has become a prominent figure in the city's progressive political movement. Raman advanced to the November 3 mayoral runoff after the June 2 primary. Certified results gave incumbent Bass 34.3%, Raman 29.0% and Spencer Pratt 25.5%. Raman's advance to the runoff turned the race into a direct contest between two Democrats. Read also | US midterms 2026: Indian-born Nithya Raman challenges LA mayor Karen Bass A McLaughlin & Associates/California Post poll conducted October 15â18 put Raman ahead by 7.9 percentage points. An Impact Research poll conducted October 2â7 put her ahead by 10 points, while a UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies/Los Angeles Times poll from September 15â20 showed an 11-point lead. Raman's candidacy is significant beyond her own electoral prospects: a victory would make her the first South Asian woman to serve as Los Angeles mayor. Her campaign will test whether her progressive coalition can expand sufficiently to defeat an incumbent in a city facing persistent housing and homelessness challenges. What's at stake for Indian-Americans For the Indian-American community, the November 3 midterms are about more than individual victories. They are a test of how far a once-underrepresented community has come in American politics â and whether its growing presence can translate into greater influence in Congress, state governments and the national debate. The stakes are particularly high for the so-called âSamosa Caucusâ, the informal label for Indian-American lawmakers in the US Congress. November 3 mideterms will shape the scale and reach of Indian-American representation in American public life. Ro Khanna, Pramila Jayapal, Ami Bera and Suhas Subramanyam are fighting to retain their House seats, while challengers such as Amish Shah and Dandiya are seeking to expand the communityâs footprint on Capitol Hill. Their outcomes will help determine whether Indian-origin representation in Congress consolidates, grows or faces a setback at a time when immigration, technology, healthcare, economic opportunity and Americaâs role in the world are fiercely contested. The stakes extend beyond Washington. Vivek Ramaswamyâs bid for governor of Ohio could take an Indian-American politician from national prominence to one of the countryâs most powerful state offices. Nirav Shahâs campaign in Maine adds another dimension to the contest for statewide leadership. Success in races such as these would signal that Indian-origin candidates are competing not just in safe districts or within established political networks, but for executive power and leadership across the political map. Yet there is no single Indian-American political story. The candidates span the ideological spectrum â from progressive Democrats to more centrist lawmakers and conservative Republicans â and are campaigning on sharply different visions of government. Their fortunes will reflect not only the strength of their personal brands and local coalitions, but also how voters respond to their parties, their policies and the national political climate. Representation, in other words, does not automatically translate into a common agenda. Ultimately, November 3 will test whether Indian-American candidates can turn growing political visibility into electoral power. The results will shape not only the careers of individual candidates, but also the scale and reach of Indian-American representation in American public life â and the influence the next generation may be able to wield in setting the countryâs political priorities. title: First Mahatma Gandhi statue in North Dakota unveiled at Bismarck's Peace Park
text: First Mahatma Gandhi statue in North Dakota unveiled at Bismarck's Peace Park. The first life-size statue of Mahatma Gandhi in North Dakota was unveiled at Peace Park in downtown Bismarck, the state's capital, in a ceremony attended by the state's first lady Kjersti Armstrong and agriculture commissioner Doug Goehring. The statue was installed with the assistance of the Consulate General of India in Seattle, with technical support from the Indian American community in North Dakota and the North Dakota Trade Office, the consulate said in a press release. The unveiling ceremony began with the national anthems of India and the United States, followed by musical renditions of Gandhi's favourite hymns by school students from North Dakota. Officials from the Bismarck Parks and Recreation District and members of the Indian American community also attended the event. The unveiling took place during the month of Gandhi Jayanti , observed worldwide on October 2 as the International Day of Non-Violence. It also marked the year of Gandhi's 157th birth anniversary. Addressing the gathering, North Dakota agriculture commissioner Doug Goehring highlighted the growing friendship between India and North Dakota. He said Gandhi's message resonated not only with India and the rest of the world but also with people in North Dakota. Goehring described the statue as a symbol of peace and non-violence and recalled Gandhi's timeless message. North Dakota first lady Kjersti Armstrong expressed her admiration for Gandhi, saying it was an honour to celebrate his legacy, which she described as being more important today than it had been in a very long time. Peace Park adds Gandhi statue to public art installations Located at 400 East Front Avenue in downtown Bismarck, Peace Park was developed shortly after the September 11, 2001, attacks. It is also home to a Peace Pole installed by the Gandhi Peace Network of North Dakota, along with other bronze sculptural artefacts. The Gandhi statue joins these installations, adding to the public art heritage of North Dakota's capital city. The consulate described Gandhi's life and message as universal symbols of peace and non-violence. The installation also comes amid growing engagement between India and North Dakota since the establishment of the Consulate General of India in Seattle. According to the consulate, visits by the Consul General to North Dakota in 2024 and 2026 included meetings with the governor, the mayor of Bismarck and leaders from the agriculture, business and education sectors. The consulate has also organised cultural and consular outreach programmes in Fargo, including the International Day of Yoga 2026 and a consular camp in February 2026. Senior delegates from the North Dakota Trade Office also visited India earlier this year as part of ongoing exchanges between the two sides. Fifth Gandhi monument under Seattle consulate's jurisdiction The Bismarck installation is the latest addition to the Consulate General of India's initiative to establish Gandhi monuments across the US Pacific North and Midwest. Watch Mahatma Gandhi Statue Restored: From Attack to Renewal on International Day of Non-Violence Earlier statues were installed at the base of the Space Needle in Seattle in October 2024, at the State Capitol in Lincoln, Nebraska, in December 2024, and at the Mansfield Center at the University of Montana in Missoula in March 2026. Along with the statue installed at Bellevue Public Library in October 2009, the Bismarck monument is the fifth Mahatma Gandhi statue within the jurisdiction of the Consulate General of India in Seattle, the press release said. title: Three days to deadline, guidelines issued for IOA's SOM nominations
text: New Delhi, Oct 10 (IANS) The Indian Olympic Association (IOA) has begun its 2026 electoral process under the National Sports Governance Act, 2025, with the Athletesâ Commission election scheduled for November 3 and the Executive Council polls set for December 5. NEW DELHI: The Indian Olympic Association (IOA) Electoral Officer (returning officer), Sanjay K. Srivastava, has issued guidelines for the Sportspersons of Outstanding Merit (SOM) elections, warning that nominations that fail to comply with the prescribed conditions will not be considered valid. In the document dated October 26, retired IAS officer Srivastava clarified the nomination procedure and issued a modified Form 2 for candidates seeking election as SOMs to the IOA General Assembly. The deadline remains October 30. Watch Bombay Sport Exchange: Mustafa Ghouse on ISL, India's sporting ecosystem and grassroots problem The revised instructions place particular emphasis on the role of proposers and seconders, who must be members of the male or female SOM roster published by the Electoral Officer on October 23. An individual can propose or second one candidate in the male category and one in the female category. However, if the same person endorses more than one candidate in either category, the later nomination will be rejected. The instructions also state that a proposer or seconder cannot withdraw their name once the nomination has been delivered. The rules permit cross-gender endorsements: a male SOM can propose or second a female candidate, and a female SOM can do the same for a male candidate. The restriction is on endorsing multiple candidates within the same category, not on the gender of the candidate being nominated. Eight representatives to enter the IOA General Assembly PT Usha The SOM election will determine eight representatives to the IOA General Assembly, comprising four men and four women. Under the IOAâs Sportspersons of Outstanding Merit Rules, 2026, one male and one female representative will subsequently be elected from among the eight to the IOA Executive Council. The SOM framework is designed to incorporate the experience of former elite athletes, including the current president PT Usha , into the governance of Indian sport. Candidates must satisfy the prescribed eligibility conditions, including Indian citizenship, being of sound mind, being between 25 and 70 years of age on the date of application, and having retired from active sport for at least one year before applying. They must also have represented India in an Olympic sport for which the concerned national sports federation or sports body is an IOA member. title: US midterms 2026: Early voting surpasses 50.5 million, Texas sees significant voter turnout increase
text: Over 50.5 million early votes cast by Saturday morning/Image: Reuters More than 50.5 million Americans have voted early ahead of the 2026 US midterm elections, nearly five million more than the total recorded during the 2022 midterms. The increase comes as both parties face closely contested races that could determine control of Congress for the final two years of President Donald Trump's second term. Data from the University of Florida's Election Lab showed that early voting had surpassed 50.5 million by Saturday morning, ahead of Tuesday's election. Among states that track voters' party affiliations, registered Democrats accounted for 10.7 million early ballots, compared with 7.8 million from registered Republicans. These figures reflect the political registration of voters who have cast ballots and do not indicate which candidates they have supported. Watch HUGE! Iran War Escalation Confirmed After Trump Defeat? Insider Discloses America's Gulf Plan The higher number of Democratic voters comes as Republicans face competitive contests in states that have traditionally favoured the party. Dissatisfaction with Trump's presidency and concerns about the cost of living have also become prominent issues in the campaign. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority in the Senate and are seeking to retain control of the chamber. Democrats are targeting traditionally Republican-leaning states, including Texas, Alaska and Kansas, where competitive races could help them secure a majority. Texas has become a major focus of the contest, with more than seven million people having already voted early, as per the University data. This is around 1.5 million more than the number recorded in the state during the 2022 midterms. The increase is also evident in Harris County, which includes Houston. By Wednesday, 862,700 people had cast early ballots there, compared with 564,500 at the same point in the 2022 election, the Associated Press analysis has found. Harris County has consistently backed Democratic candidates in recent elections. In 2024, Kamala Harris defeated Trump in the county by nearly six percentage points in the presidential election. Democratic Senate candidate Colin Allred also won the county by roughly 11 percentage points over Republican incumbent Ted Cruz. This year's Texas Senate contest has drawn national attention, with Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton facing Democratic candidate James Talarico. Republican Governor Greg Abbott is also seeking re-election against Democrat Gina Hinojosa. Early voting has also increased in other states with competitive Senate races. South Carolina, which Trump won by nearly 18 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election, has recorded an 83% rise in early voting compared with the 2022 midterms, as per AP analysis. In Kansas, where Republicans face another closely contested Senate race, early voting is up 34%. Maine has recorded a 44% increase, while Michigan has seen a rise of 32%, the AP reported. The midterm elections will determine the composition of the House of Representatives and Senate for the remaining two years of Trump's term. Rising prices of food, petrol and other essentials, the war involving Iran and concerns about government corruption have featured in the political debate ahead of the vote. Trump has held rallies across several states to support Republican candidates, including in areas that have traditionally been considered safe for the party. During his campaign appearances, he has repeatedly commented on candidates' physical appearance and dismissed concerns about rising petrol prices, pointing instead to the profits of fossil fuel companies. Speaking at a rally in Florida on Friday night, Trump acknowledged the demands of his campaign schedule. âI thought this was it,â he said. âI thought I could relax. title: EPS demands reopening of Amma Clinics
text: Chennai: AIADMK general secretary Edappadi K Palaniswami has demanded that chief minister C Joseph Vijay reopen Amma Clinics to shield people from exorbitant prices fixed by drug companies. He also chaired a district secretariesâ meeting in Chennai where rebel leaders S P Velumani and Natham Viswanathan were absent. Former police officer S Velladurai joined the party on the sidelines of the district secretariesâ meeting, triggering speculation that he might be fielded as the partyâs bypoll candidate in Ambasamudram. Velladurai, who retired from service in 2024, had turned a supporter of V K Sasikala . He was fielded as a candidate of All India Puratchi Thalaivar Makkal Munnetra Kazhagam headed by her in the 2026 assembly election in Nanguneri assembly constituency. However, he was defeated. With Sasikala herself distancing herself from AIPTMMK, Velladurai has opted to join AIADMK. âChief minister C Joseph Vijay cannot be compared to MGR (the late CM M G Ramachandran). MGR was a mountain, but the CM now is just a mound,â he told reporters. AIADMK functionaries said the subject of bypolls did come up during the district secretariesâ meeting, but candidates were not discussed. âLet the announcement of elections come, we shall speak about it after that,â Palaniswami told reporters after the meeting when asked whether AIADMK was prepared for the bypolls. Earlier in the day, he cited a report on rising drug prices and flayed TVK govt for not reopening Amma Clinics. Palaniswami said the state govt was keen on increasing liquor prices but the same attention was not given to pharmacies. title: Trump gives reporter fitness lecture as MAGA loses shape
text: The exchange was not merely an illustration of a President with an unusually short fuse that has been sizzling lately; it was also a revealing snapshot of a leader entering the final stretch of an election campaign with considerably more anxiety than his public bravado suggests. (Photo: AP) TOI Correspondent from Washington: Four days before a midterm election that could leave him politically out of shape, US President Donald Trump decided to conduct a fitness assessment --- of a Reuters journalist. Faced with an innocuous question about why he was cancelling campaign rallies in Kansas and Iowa, the MAGA boss erupted into an unsolicited lecture on the journalist's weight, appearance, and general state of health, betraying frayed nerves that do not augur well for his party. âYou are a sick guy! Reuters is terrible, by the way. Look at this guy... he's way out of shape... You are disgusting! Put yourself in shape! You look like hell!â Trump exploded at the reporter, pushing back at any suggestion that he was tired or backing out of rallies because of heckling and poor attendance. He said he felt great and the reason he was not going to those states was because Republican candidates were doing very well and his energies were better devoted elsewhere. The exchange was not merely an illustration of a President with an unusually short fuse that has been sizzling lately; it was also a revealing snapshot of a leader entering the final stretch of an election campaign with considerably more anxiety than his public bravado suggests. Polls show Democratic candidates leading, tied, or narrowing margins in the most unexpected places, including ruby red states Trump won by 10 to 20 points in the 2024 Presidential elections. For instance, in Kansas, a state that has not elected a Democrat Senator since 1932, polls put Democrat Adam Hamilton ahead of incumbent Roger Marshall 49-45. Texas, which last elected a Democrat Senator in 1988 and which Trump carried comfortably in 2024, has become a genuine Senate battleground, with Democrat James Talarico -- who incidentally was ladling out dosas on Thursday in an effort to court Indian-American votes --- ahead of Republican Ken Paxton. South Carolina, where Republican Darline Graham is hoping to succeed her late brother Lindsay Graham as senator, has also tightened considerably. Even more unnerving for Republicans are the warning signs from states that have traditionally been considered political fortresses, including Louisiana and Mississippi, which last elected a Democratic senator in 1982. If Dems win all these races, they would be on track to reverse the Republicansâ 53-47 control of the Senate, A Democratic takeover of both chambers would leave Trump facing not merely hostile congressional hearings but chambers capable of blocking appointments, frustrating legislation, and investigating an administration dogged by allegations of cronyism and self-enrichment. Republicans, naturally, have a theory about why the polls are wrong: the hidden Trump voter. They argue that there are millions of Trump supporters who refuse to participate in polls, conceal their preferences or simply do not admit to pollsters that they intend to vote Republican. They will emerge, the theory goes, on Election Day and deliver the customary surprise. But hoping for invisible voters is not quite the same as having visible enthusiasm. In fact, some of the most visible activity at recent Trump rallies has been distinctly uncomfortable for the president and his MAGA faithful. Hecklers have interrupted Trump's speeches at rallies and his surrogates have been pranked on several occasions. At an Ohio rally, a comedian who goes by the name Robby Roadsteamer managed to interrupt Trump with a reference to Jeffrey Epstein, before being escorted out amid chants of "USA!USA!" a standard MAGA response. The president's explanation was that such protesters were paid by radical left political enemies. Roadstreamer meanwhile took credit for Trump's subsequent cancellation of the Kansas and Iowa appearances, announcing online: âTrump cancelled the rest of his rallies! You're welcome, America.â Trump allies, including Vivek Ramaswamy and Fox News, have also been punked by pranksters, who present themselves as MAGA loyalists before turning on them on camera. Trump's own response to the heckling and harsh scrutiny by the mainstream media has been to crank the personal insults up another notch, with consequent blowback that is raising political temperature all around. When he suggested that Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed should have to pass through a metal detector before entering the Senate (suggesting he is a jihadist who cannot be trusted), the Michigan Democrat clapped back: âI'll go through a metal detector if you'll sit for a lie detectorâ -- to answer questions about his ties to Epstein. Trump has also repeatedly disparaged Texas' Democratic candidate James Talarico as "Tala-freako" -- part of his chronic habit of name-calling. There is a broader political backdrop to the president's increasingly irritable demeanour. His administration is facing mounting accusations of corruption, grift, and self-dealing, while its aggressive efforts to influence election processes have raised questions about whether Trump is prepared to accept an adverse outcome in the election. Past record does not inspire any great confidence. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

title: 2 yrs, 122 days of protests later, PU still awaits Senate
text: Two years, 122 days of stir later, PU still awaits Senate Chandigarh: Nearly two years after Panjab Universityâs previous Senate completed its tenure, 122 days of protests over its governing structure and a year-long standoff later, the university still awaits the formal constitution of its new 91-member Senate. The electoral process concluded on Oct 4, but Nov 1, the traditional date for commencement of the Senateâs four-year tenure, has passed without the 47 elected fellows being formally notified or the 36 members to be nominated by Vice-President CP Radhakrishnan, the university Chancellor, being announced. The previous Senateâs four-year tenure ended on Oct 31, 2024, without fresh elections being held. The absence of an elected House triggered a 96-day agitation by students under the Panjab University Bachao Morcha. The issue took another turn in Oct 2025 when the Centre proposed restructuring the Senate and Syndicate by reducing the Senateâs size and changing its composition. The move triggered widespread opposition on campus and another 26-day protest. The Centre eventually withdrew the changes on Nov 7, 2025, and the Vice-President approved the election schedule on Nov 27, ending the immediate deadlock over holding the polls. The Senate comprises 91 members, including 47 elected fellows, 36 nominated by the Chancellor, two members nominated by the Punjab legislative assembly and six ex-officio members. While results for the elected constituencies have been declared, their formal approval and notification by the Chancellor are awaited. The list of 36 nominated members is also pending. Prof Rajat Sandhir, elected from the Combined Faculties constituency, said there should be no further delay in constituting the Senate. âThe notification should be issued immediately so that Panjab University has its governing body in place. The Senate is the universityâs highest statutory authority and important decisions concerning the institution need to be deliberated upon and taken through this body. There is no reason for the process to be held up any further,â he said. Simranjit Singh Dhillon, elected from the Registered Graduates constituency, said the delay was unjustified, particularly after the university had already remained without an elected Senate for nearly two years. âIt is absolutely unjustified that such delays continue even after the election process has been completed. The university has already lost considerable time without an elected Senate. Any further delay does not send the right signal. The notification should come without any more waiting,â he said. Jodh Singh, also elected from the Registered Graduates constituency, said the Senate should be constituted and convened before the Vice-Presidentâs proposed visit to the university in Dec. âThe Senate should be in place before the Vice-Presidentâs visit. Important decisions taken by the present and previous vice-chancellors during the period when the elected Senate was absent should be placed before the House for discussion and appropriate consideration. The university cannot continue functioning indefinitely without its elected governing body,â he said. In the absence of the Senate, important university decisions have been handled through committees and other administrative mechanisms rather than an elected House. Once the Senate is notified, the university will also be able to initiate the process of constituting the Syndicate, its executive body, through elections among senators. The elected representatives are now seeking early notification of both categories of members so that the new House can be convened and resume its statutory functions.
