title: US midterms 2026: Meet Vivek Ramaswamy, Trump-backed Republican seeking the Ohio governorship
text: Ramaswamy has recently faced bipartisan criticism over a campaign advertisement. President Donald Trump-backed Indian-American Republican Vivek Ramaswamy rose to prominence during the 2024 US presidential race, positioning himself as a bold, unconventional candidate. He challenged Trump for the Republican nomination before suspending his campaign in January 2024 and endorsing him. Ramaswamy remains a prominent figure in business and politics and is now the Republican candidate for Ohio governor. He will face Democratic nominee Amy Acton in the November 3 2026, general election. The 40-year-old biotech entrepreneur has recently faced bipartisan criticism over a campaign advertisement featuring Acton's estranged mother, Donna Arthur, who calls her daughter a liar. Ramaswamy has defended the advertisement, saying it is about alleged dishonesty rather than Acton's childhood abuse. Watch 'HE NEEDS A METAL DETECTOR!' Trump Targets El-Sayed At Michigan Rally, Calls Him 'Jihadist' Who is Vivek Ramaswamy? Born on August 9, 1985, in Cincinnati, Ohio, Vivek Ramaswamy is the son of Indian immigrants from Kerala who moved to the US in the 1970s. His mother was a geriatric psychiatrist, while his father worked as an engineer and patent lawyer at General Electric. Ramaswamy grew up with his younger brother, Shankar, and graduated as the valedictorian of his Jesuit high school. He was also a nationally ranked junior tennis player and an accomplished pianist. Ramaswamy graduated summa cum laude from Harvard University in 2007 with a degree in biology. He later worked in life sciences investing before earning a law degree from Yale Law School in 2013. He met his future wife, Apoorva Tewari, a medical student who later became a throat surgeon, while studying at Yale. In 2014, at the age of 29, Ramaswamy founded Roivant Sciences, a biopharmaceutical company focused on developing medicines. His business ventures helped him build substantial wealth and establish himself in the biotechnology industry. He later gained national attention for his criticism of environmental, social and governance (ESG) investing, arguing that companies should focus on business performance rather than social and political causes. His views, frequent media appearances and book Woke, Inc. helped raise his profile in conservative political circles. Ramaswamy's presidential bid and ties with Trump Ramaswamy announced his candidacy for Ohio governor in February 2025 and received Trump's endorsement. His campaign has focused on economic opportunity, tax cuts and education reform. Among his proposals are eliminating Ohio's state income tax, reducing property taxes and raising academic standards in public schools. He has also pledged to engage with voters across all 88 counties in the state. Ramaswamy won the Republican primary in May 2026 and will face Acton, a physician and former director of the Ohio Department of Health, in the general election. Why is Ramaswamy facing backlash over his campaign ad? The controversy centres on an advertisement featuring Acton's estranged mother, Donna Arthur, who accuses her daughter of lying and questions her account of her childhood. Acton has spoken publicly about experiencing homelessness and abuse as a child. Her stepfather was indicted on charges of raping her when she was 12, after her biological father reported the allegations. Acton and her brother were removed from their mother's custody. Her stepfather pleaded not guilty and later died. Ramaswamy defended the advertisement at a campaign stop in northeast Ohio, saying it had nothing to do with childhood abuse. âThe irony is theyâre lying about an ad that is about lying,â he said, the Associated Press reported. âTheyâre changing the subject because they donât want to answer for their own failures." Acton condemned the advertisement, telling Spectrum News, âI wonât normalize somebody who has said that my childhood is just something Iâm complaining about.â The advertisement has drawn criticism from Republicans and Democrats. Ohio Governor Mike DeWine called for it to be taken down, saying, âItâs wrong to run this ad.â Trump, however, backed the campaign's approach, describing the advertisement as âhitting pay dirtâ. Vice-President JD Vance also defended Ramaswamy, criticising Republicans who objected to the ad. The controversy has brought renewed national attention to the Ohio governor's race ahead of the November 3 election. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

title: Maldives opposition's possible presidential pick Abdulla Shahid held in child abuse case
text: Shahid served as the Maldives' foreign affairs minister between 2018 and 2023 under former president Ibrahim Mohamed Solih. During this period, he also became one of the country's most recognisable faces in international diplomacy. Former Maldives foreign affairs minister Abdulla Shahid, was arrested on suspicion of sexually abusing a minor, the Maldives Police said on Monday. Notably, the 64-year-old former president of the United Nations General Assembly who was emerging as a potential presidential challenger to incumbent Mohamed Muizzu in the 2028 elections. He was taken into custody in MalÃ© at around 9.59pm local time on Monday under a court warrant. Shahid has rejected the allegations, calling them baseless and politically motivated. The arrest comes at a crucial time for the opposition Maldivian Democratic Party (MDP), which is preparing for the next presidential election. Shahid was considered one of the prominent contenders for the party's presidential nomination. The Maldives Police confirmed the arrest in a statement posted on X. "On suspicion of sexually abusing a child under the age of 18, Abdulla Shahid (64 yrs), H. Rabeeâee Manzil, MalÃ©, was arrested under a court warrant on the night of 2 November 2026, at around 21:59. The police are currently conducting further investigations into this case," the police said. The police have not disclosed further details about the allegations. They said investigations into the case are continuing. Shahid rejects allegations Following his arrest, Shahid denied the allegations and accused those circulating the claims of attempting to damage his reputation. In a post on X, he said: "The stories being politically circulated to assassinate my character are completely baseless lies. I urge everyone to refrain from spreading such unsubstantiated claims," The former minister has not publicly provided further details about the allegations or the circumstances leading to his arrest. The police have also not shared additional information about the case. Who is Abdulla Shahid, Muizzu's potential challenger Shahid is among the Maldives' most prominent political figures and has held several senior positions in the country's government and political establishment. He served as the Maldives' foreign affairs minister between 2018 and 2023 under former president Ibrahim Mohamed Solih. His most prominent international role came when he presided over the 76th session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) during 2021-22. He was also the Speaker of the People's Majlis, the Maldives' parliament, and headed the opposition MDP from February 2024 until August 2026. Shahid stepped down as MDP president in August 2026 to contest the party's presidential primary. He was subsequently seen as a prominent potential candidate for the party's nomination ahead of the 2028 presidential election. The arrest could therefore have significant political implications for the opposition party as it prepares to challenge President Mohamed Muizzu. Shahid's political position and MDP's preparations for 2028 The MDP is one of the Maldives' principal political parties and was in power under former president Ibrahim Mohamed Solih from 2018 to 2023. Solih lost the 2023 presidential election to Muizzu, who contested as the candidate of the People's National Congress (PNC). With the next presidential election scheduled for 2028, the opposition has been preparing to regain power. Shahid's international profile and experience in government had placed him among the prominent names being considered for the party's presidential nomination. However, the criminal allegations and his arrest could complicate his political prospects. The investigation is still underway, and the allegations against him have not been established. title: US midterms 2026: How 9/11 shaped Saritha Komatireddyâs legal career as she runs for New York attorney general
text: Saritha Komatireddy is among the Indian-origin candidates contesting the US midterm elections on November 3. A former assistant attorney in the Eastern District of New York, she is the Republican nominee for New York attorney general and will challenge two-time incumbent Letitia James, the Democratic Party nominee. Among her prominent backers is US President Donald Trump, who nominated Komatireddy for a federal judgeship in the Eastern District of New York in May 2020, during his first term in office. Family life Komatireddyâs parents immigrated to the United States from what is now Telangana, in southern India, during the 1980s. Born in Brooklyn, New York, she spent part of her childhood in Missouri. In an interview with The Wall Street Journal, Komatireddy spoke about her father's humble beginnings in India and his decision to immigrate to the United States. âMy dad is from a small village in India that had no running water, and he left India when it was a socialist country. He came here for the same reason many New Yorkersâ families come here: work hard, dream big and have a shot at achieving your dreams," she said. How 9/11 changed her life According to Komatireddy, the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks in New York City shaped her decision to pursue a career in law, with a focus on prosecuting terrorists and protecting national security. âMy first week in college, terrorists attacked New York. 9/11 changed my life. I chose law school to prosecute terrorists, to protect New York and America,â she said in her campaign video. Komatireddy graduated from both Harvard College and Harvard Law School. She began her legal career as a law clerk to Brett Kavanaugh, who was then a judge on the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit and now serves as an associate justice of the US Supreme Court. Professional career According to her campaign website, Komatireddy spent more than a decade prosecuting cases involving leaders of Al-Qaeda, ISIS and Mexican drug cartels. As a federal prosecutor in the Eastern District of New York, she handled high-profile cases involving international terrorism, cybercrime, narcotics trafficking, money laundering, fraud and foreign public corruption. From 2023 to 2024, she served as chief of staff of the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) under then-President Joe Biden. Komatireddy, a mother of four, is a partner at the law firm Holtzman Vogel and teaches at Columbia University. title: Two Indians among 28 green card holders charged with election fraud in California
text: 1. Two Indians face US election fraud charges over 2024 voting (Representative image: Reuters photo) Two Indian nationals are among 28 green card holders charged with election-related offences in California, including fraudulent voter registration and voting in the November 2024 US elections, the US Department of Justice said on Monday. The accused Indians have been identified as Amandeep Kaur, 30, a resident of Rancho Palos Verdes, and Kamlesh Shah, 67, who lives in Sacramento. It was not immediately clear whether either of them was among the 11 people arrested during early morning raids across California under âOperation Protect the Voteâ. According to the Justice Department, Shah fraudulently registered to vote on the day of the November 2024 general election and cast his ballot the same day. Kaur, who is seeking US citizenship, allegedly registered to vote in December 2022 and voted in the November 2024 election. âAll 28 foreign nationals charged are lawful permanent residents (LPRs), or 'green card' holders. Although LPRs have legal immigration status in the United States, they are not US citizens and are not permitted to vote in US elections,â the Justice Department said. The charges include making false statements in naturalisation applications and fraudulent voter registration. Both offences are felonies that carry a maximum penalty of five years in federal prison. DOJ links accused to voter registration list Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said all 28 defendants appeared on a list of more than 20,000 people the Justice Department had provided to California election officials the previous week. âEach of the 28 defendants charged today appears on the list of more than 20,000 likely noncitizen registrants we provided to California election officials last week,â McCotter told reporters in Los Angeles. The charges come amid an escalating dispute between the Trump administration and California officials over allegations of non-citizen voter registration. The Justice Department has also asked a federal court to prevent California and Los Angeles County from processing ballots returned by people on the list, arguing that votes cast illegally could undermine election integrity. California officials have opposed the demand, saying the federal government has not provided sufficient evidence to establish that those listed are non-citizens. They have also argued that withholding or refusing to count ballots could violate federal and state law and disenfranchise eligible voters. Trump administration steps up election investigations The Justice Department has intensified investigations into alleged election-related offences as early voting begins in several states. Before Mondayâs announcement, it had charged about 90 people with various forms of election misconduct this year, including 50 accused of voting as non-citizens. The department said on Monday that it had charged 113 non-citizens across 20 states with voting and registration offences over the preceding seven weeks. Election law experts have cautioned that such cases do not establish widespread non-citizen voting. They have also warned that aggressive efforts to scrutinise voter rolls could risk removing eligible voters or undermining public confidence in elections. California officials have questioned the Justice Departmentâs methodology for identifying the 20,000 people, while the federal government has argued that access to additional voter registration data would help verify their citizenship status. title: Andhra Pradesh urban polls set to become first mid-term test for NDA govt
text: Around one crore voters are eligible to cast their votes in 100 urban local bodies going to polls on Sunday. The electorate accounts for nearly a quarter of the stateâs voters and spans around 60 assembly constituencies, making the outcome politically significant for both the ruling alliance and the opposition Vijayawada : The urban local body elections scheduled for Sunday are set to be the first major political test for the ruling NDA coalition since it came to power with a near sweep in the 2024 assembly elections. More than a civic contest, the polls are being viewed as a mid-term assessment of the Chandrababu Naidu-led NDA govtâs performance over the last two-and-a-half years and an opportunity for the opposition YSRCP to gauge its prospects of a political resurgence. The NDAâs landslide victory in the 2024 elections, when it won 164 of the 175 assembly seats and reduced the YSRCP to just 11 seats, fundamentally altered Andhra Pradesh âs political landscape. The municipal elections will be the first occasion on which the ruling coalition seeks a fresh mandate from voters after assuming office. The significance of the exercise extends beyond the urban local bodies, and rural local body elections are scheduled to follow next. This effectively brings the entire electorate of the state back to the polling booth. Political parties therefore view the municipal polls as an early indicator of public mood ahead of a larger electoral cycle. Around one crore voters are eligible to cast their votes in 100 urban local bodies going to polls on Sunday. The electorate accounts for nearly a quarter of the stateâs voters and spans around 60 assembly constituencies, making the outcome politically significant for both the ruling alliance and the opposition. Although municipal elections are traditionally fought on civic issues such as roads, drainage, sanitation, drinking water and urban infrastructure, the campaign in Andhra Pradesh has largely revolved around broader political narratives. In several towns and cities, parties framed the election as a contest between the NDA govtâs performance and the YSRCPâs bid for a comeback rather than a debate on local governance. The intensity of the campaign, particularly in parts of Rayalaseema, has reflected the high political stakes involved. Reports of clashes and confrontations during the filing of nominations and campaigning underscored the extent to which the elections have transcended civic issues and assumed the character of a larger political battle. For the NDA, retaining dominance in urban local bodies is crucial. A favourable verdict would be seen as public endorsement of govtâs performance and a validation of the coalitionâs governance agenda. The results will also be closely scrutinised for evidence of how effectively votes are being transferred among the alliance partners â TDP, Jana Sena and BJP â at the grassroots level. The elections are equally important for the YSRCP, which is attempting to recover from its worst electoral defeat. Despite the collapse in seat share in the 2024 assembly polls, the party retained roughly 40% of the vote share statewide. YSRCP leaders believe the municipal elections could provide an opportunity to demonstrate that the party continues to enjoy substantial voter support despite its diminished legislative presence. title: Gyanesh has to go, PM & Shah next, says Rahul Gandhi at anti-CEC rally
text: Around 50,000 people turned up for INDIA blocâs rally in Delhi on Sunday, according to Delhi Police estimates NEW DELHI: In a Ramlila Maidan packed with protesters and ringing with anti-BJP and anti-CEC slogans Sunday, Congress MP Rahul Gandhi said the opposition will confront the top BJP duo of Narendra Modi and Amit Shah after Gyanesh Kumar's removal as chief election commissioner. The trio was losing sleep over the agitation, he claimed, and said the CEC's exit would be the first step in putting the country back on track. With opposition biggies Congress chief Mallikarjun Kharge, Sonia Gandhi, Akhilesh Yadav, Mamata Banerjee, Tejashwi Yadav, Dipankar Bhattacharya, MA Baby, Farooq Abdullah and Mehbooba Mufti on the dais, leader of opposition in Lok Sabha said the "voice of the people of India" is greater to him than religion, and he will brook no assault on it. Mocking BJP's catchphrase - "Modi kahin nahin jayega" - which was coined in response to Kharge's comment, Rahul said the PM won't be allowed to go anywhere. "You cannot flee... You will stay here and face action." 2024 polls illegal, says Rahul; Modi picking voters: Kharge With a âvote bachao, desh bachaoâ banner forming the backdrop of the dais, the speakers focused on âvote choriâ, repeating allegations about SIR and deletion of around 14 crore voters. Rahul accused the CEC, PM and Shah of suppressing the voice of people through âvote choriâ. While Mamata and Akhilesh said the West Bengal mandate to BJP was âstolenâ, Rahul mentioned the Maharashtra, Haryana, Chhattisgarh, MP and 2024 Lok Sabha polls. He said the 2024 polls were illegal, arguing the difference between NDA and opposition was merely 3%, while 15% of the 2024 voters have been deleted under SIR. âModi is selecting the voters,â Congress chief Kharge said. Led by Kharge, most INDIA bloc members stressed ejecting BJP from office was a must to save democracy, even leading the crowd in âBJP hatao, desh bachaoâ chants. Some reminded the crowd that Ramlila Maidan has been the harbinger of history and change in the past. SP chief Akhilesh called the historic venue the âHaldighati of democracyâ, referring to the battlefield in Rajasthan where Maharana Pratap faced off with the Mughals in 1576, remembered as a symbol of defiant resistance to a powerful empire. Addressing the crowd that had been growing since 9am and remained eager even as main INDIA bloc members came on the dais only by 3pm, Akhilesh, who occupied a key spot with UP polls looming, hit out at Modi, saying, âJo UP se aaye the, woh UP se hi jaayenge (those who came from UP, will go from UP)â. Watch âGyanesh Kumar Is Modiâs Puppetâ: Tejashwi Yadavâs âMahabharataâ Attack At Anti-SIR Rally âThe UP poll results will see off BJP from office in Lucknow and Delhi,â he said, also raising âchanda choriâ in Ayodhya in his speech. Akhilesh warned BJP was constantly trying to steal elections, even blaming SPâs 2022 assembly defeat on voter list manipulation. The SP chief said UP BJP has stated that 1.27 crore votes of Hindus have been deleted in UP. He said the statement seems designed to âput the blame for their upcoming defeat on someone elseâ â touching upon the much-talked about âDelhi vs Lucknowâ faultlines in BJP. Indulging the sloganeering crowd, Rahul said his predictions always come true, and he was now forecasting that CEC Kumar would go to jail. âVote choriâ is no smalltime shoplifting but a ârarest of rare caseâ which qualifies as âtreasonâ, Rahul said. âWithout Gyanesh, Modi would not be PM and Shah would not be HM. He also accused RSS of capturing all institutions, including judiciary and bureaucracy, while âtwo or three people like Ambani and Adani have cornered all the wealthâ. title: 82% disapprove of Trump. So why are fewer Indian-Americans identifying as Democrats?
text: US midterms are set to be held on November 3 At an Indian restaurant in Irving, near Dallas, Democratic US Senate candidate James Talarico tried his hand at making a masala dosa , spreading batter on a hot pan and filling it with spiced potatoes. In Connecticut, Governor Ned Lamont joined Diwali celebrations, while Republican Congressman John James visited a Swaminarayan temple in Michigan. From dosas to Diwali and temple visits, politicians from both parties are making symbolic overtures to Indian-American voters ahead of the November 3 midterms. But the communityâs political allegiances are not as straightforward as those campaign gestures might suggest. At the national level, Republicans are fighting hard to retain control of both chambers of Congress. And the odds, at least in prediction markets, are not in their favour. As of October 30, betting website Kalshi gave Democrats a 92% chance of taking control of the House of Representatives and a 69% chance of winning the Senate. Polymarket's corresponding figures were 94% and 72%. A Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on October 26 also found Democrats leading Republicans 47% to 36% among registered voters. Losing control of either chamber, or in the worst case both, could severely hamper US President Donald Trump 's legislative agenda in the final two years of his presidency. So the stakes couldn't be higher . With the Trump administration pursuing what many see as anti-immigration policies, the stakes are also fairly high for the 5.2 million people of Indian origin living in the US. However, there is an interesting paradox between their voting patterns and declared political affiliations. While most are strongly anti-Trump, many don't identify as Democrats. The party's perceived leftward tilt appears to be one source of discomfort among some Indian-Americans. An AP-NORC and AAPI Data survey released on October 19 found that 82% of Indian-American respondents disapprove of Trump's job performance. Yet four in ten held an unfavourable opinion of the Democrats. A separate series of surveys by the Carnegie Endowment earlier in the year suggests that fewer Indian-Americans identify as Democrats than they did six years ago, while more describe themselves as independents. Trump gets thumbs down Together, the surveys challenge the idea of Indian-Americans as a politically uniform community. They reveal differences across age, education, income and other factors that shape political affiliation. A clear Democratic lead The AP-NORC/AAPI Data survey, conducted from September 8 to 15, found Trump's handling of the economy similarly unpopular: 81% disapproved and 18% approved. On immigration, 70% disapproved of his performance. Almost in lockstep, the Republican Party was viewed favourably by only 19%, while 70% held an unfavourable opinion of it. Democrats were in a substantially stronger position, with 51% viewing the party favourably. That advantage also appears in surveys measuring voting intentions. The 2026 AAPI Voter Survey, conducted by AAPI Data and APIAVote between June and July, found that 66% of Indian-American registered voters preferred Democratic candidates for the House of Representatives, against 18% favouring Republicans. Democratic Senate candidates also attracted 66%, compared with 22% for Republicans. Fewer are calling themselves Democrats According to the Carnegie Endowment's 2026 Indian-American Attitudes Survey, conducted between November 2025 and January 2026, the share of Indian-American adults identifying as Democrats declined from 52% in 2020 to 48% in 2024 and 46% in 2026. Over the same period, Republican identification rose from 15% to 19%, while independent identification increased from 23% to 29%. Republicans' gains came between 2020 and 2024; between 2024 and 2026, their share of party identifiers remained unchanged at 19%. The independent share, meanwhile, rose four percentage points. The two-point dip in Democratic identification during this period is small relative to the survey's margin of error. Being independent, however, does not mean being undecided, particularly given the two-party nature of US politics. Carnegie found that the independent share dropped from 29% to 17% when respondents were offered the option of leaning towards one of the two parties. The ideological picture offers another clue. Carnegie found that 32% of Indian-Americans identified as moderates in 2026, up from 28% in 2024. The share selecting the specific label 'liberal' declined from 25% to 21%. But when those identifying as slightly liberal and extremely liberal are included, the broader liberal segment has changed little over the past six years. Rather than indicating a conservative shift, Carnegie describes the community as broadly centrist, with a left-of-centre tilt. Fewer Indian Americans identify as Dems On a scale of zero to 100, the Democratic Party's average rating in Carnegie's survey fell from 60 in 2024 to 53 in 2026. The Republican Party's rating also dropped, from 41 to 34. The decline extended to leading political figures. Kamala Harris's average rating fell from 62 to 52, while Trump's dropped from 40 to 32. Exhausted, but engaged There is another striking finding from the AAPI Voter Survey. Although 92% of Indian-American registered voters said they planned to vote in November, 66% said they always (29%) or often (37%) felt exhausted when thinking about politics. At the same time, 43% described themselves as more enthusiastic than usual about voting in the midterms, compared with 22% who were less enthusiastic, perhaps because a lot more is at stake now. Three-quarters of respondents said they had discussed politics with family or friends in the previous year. Another 25% had discussed politics or community issues through group messaging platforms such as WhatsApp, while 24% had posted about politics on social media. But direct party outreach tells a different story. Forty percent of Indian-American registered voters reported receiving no contact from the Democratic Party over the preceding year, while 56% said the same of Republicans. The Democratic drift is not uniform Carnegie's findings also challenge the idea that younger Indian-Americans are necessarily moving away from Democrats. Among respondents aged 18 to 29, Democratic identification increased from 51% in 2024 to 56% in 2026. Among those aged 50 and above, however, it declined from 47% to 39%. Education produced another divide. Democratic identification among respondents without a college degree fell from 48% to 35%, while remaining broadly unchanged among college graduates, at 49%. Income revealed a similar split. Among Indian-Americans in households earning between $50,000 and $99,999 annually, Democratic identification declined from 54% to 44%. Among those in households earning at least $100,000, it increased from 46% to 51%. Gender differences were also visible. Democratic identification among men fell from 46% to 40%, while among women it rose slightly, from 50% to 52%. So older Indian-Americans appear to be moving away from identifying as card-carrying Democrats, although the trend among the well-off is different. Economy remains the big issue In the September AP-NORC/AAPI Data poll, 87% of Indian-American respondents identified the economy as one of the most important election issues. Cost of living followed at 84%, while 76% said the same of healthcare. Despite weaker party identification, Democrats enjoyed sizeable advantages on these issues. Fifty-three percent trusted Democrats more to handle the economy, compared with 12% who trusted Republicans. On the cost of living, the corresponding figures were 52% and 8%. On healthcare, Democrats held an even larger advantage, with 60% trusting them more, against just 6% for Republicans. But these preferences did not amount to universal confidence in the party. On the economy, 20% trusted neither party. On the cost of living, the proportion was 25%. Economy to healthcare: Democrats enjoy a clear lead Democrats also had an advantage on immigration in the September survey, with 50% trusting them more, against 18% who preferred Republicans. On crime, however, the numerical gap was narrower: 29% trusted Democrats more and 19% Republicans, while 28% trusted neither. India ties not a major concern Inflation and prices were the single most important policy issue for 21% of respondents in Carnegie's survey, followed by jobs and the economy at 17%. Healthcare ranked next at 13%, followed by immigration at 11%. Only 2% named USâIndia relations as their top concern. That is perhaps along expected lines, though many in India probably view Indian-Americans' political behaviour through the prism of the IndiaâUS bilateral relationship. For most desis living in the US, it is not the top concern. The finding does not mean that Indian-Americans are indifferent to relations between Washington and New Delhi. It means that domestic issues, particularly economic concerns, matter more when respondents are asked to identify their single most important policy priority. Is the Democratic Party's leftward tilt a problem? Carnegie asked respondents who did not identify as Democrats to rank their top two objections to the party. The most frequently cited reason, at 19%, was the perception that Democrats were too influenced by their left wing. Concerns about the party's approach to illegal immigration and disagreements with its economic policies followed at 17% each. Another 16% cited perceptions that Democrats were too soft on crime, while an equal share objected to what they considered excessive emphasis on identity politics. These issues overlap with broader conservative criticism of what is often called liberal or 'woke' politics. The findings suggest that the Democratic Party's perceived leftward tilt makes it harder for some Indian-Americans to identify with the party. But there is another side to this argument. The same Carnegie survey found that 68% of Indian-Americans who were familiar with Zohran Mamdani were enthusiastic about his election as New York City mayor, while 22% were unenthusiastic. Among those enthusiastic about his victory, 44% cited the expectation that he would govern as a liberal or progressive. Among those unenthusiastic, 36% said he was too liberal or progressive. Even among Indian-Americans identifying as Republicans, enthusiasm and opposition to Mamdani's victory were almost evenly divided, at 44% and 45%, respectively. That makes the political picture more complicated. Some Indian-Americans regard the Democratic Party as too influenced by its left wing, while others welcome the rise of progressive politicians such as Mamdani. The question beyond November 3 There are important limitations to these findings. The relatively small ethnic subgroups surveyed carry greater statistical uncertainty than the surveys' overall samples. Carnegie's historical survey waves also involved different respondents and changes in sampling methods, so the reported shifts do not establish that individual voters have switched party allegiance. What the surveys do show is a distinction between candidate preference and party identity. Democratic candidates continue to enjoy a large advantage. Trump's job performance is viewed negatively by a substantial majority. Beyond the midterms, the challenge for Democrats will be to sustain their electoral support among Indian-Americans while addressing the concerns of those who no longer identify strongly with the party. Attention will eventually turn to the nomination contests ahead of the 2028 presidential election. The continuing influence of the MAGA movement within the Republican Party, and the ideological direction of the Democrats, will be among the factors shaping the political choices facing Indian-Americans. For now, though, the polling suggests that many desis would like to give Trump the electoral blues. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

title: HC admits BJP petition challenging Narla MLAâs election
text: Orissa high court Cuttack : Orissa high court has kept alive a legal challenge to the 2024 election of Narla MLA Manorama Mohanty of BJD, admitting a petition by BJP candidate Aniruddha Pradhan seeking to take over the election case withdrawn by former Congress candidate Bhakta Charan Das. Justice Sashikanta Mishra, while hearing Pradhanâs petition on Oct 30, treated service of notice on Mohanty as sufficient after she reportedly refused to accept it. âOffice note indicates that notice sent to the respondent (Manorama Mohanty) was refused. Hence, the same is treated as sufficient. List this matter on 11.11.2026,â the judge ordered. Pradhan, who finished third in the 2024 Assembly election from Narla, has sought permission to substitute himself as the petitioner in place of Das, who had challenged Mohantyâs election. The court had issued notice to the sitting BJD MLA on Aug 19. The BJP candidate has questioned the manner in which Das was allowed to withdraw his election petition, alleging that mandatory procedures under the Representation of the People Act, 1951, were not followed. He contended that no gazette notification, required under Sections 109(2), 110(3)(b) and 111 of the Act, was published following the withdrawal. Pradhan argued that the omission deprived him and other voters of an opportunity to object to the withdrawal or seek substitution. He relied on Section 110(3)(c), which allows a candidate who contested the election to seek substitution in place of a petitioner withdrawing an election challenge. He has also sought continuation of the original allegations against Mohanty, particularly that her nomination papers were improperly accepted because of alleged misinformation or suppression of material particulars about her educational qualification in the election affidavit. Pradhan claimed oral and documentary evidence had already been placed before the court and said the issue involved public interest. Das, who is also Odisha Pradesh Congress Committee president and a former MP, had lost the Narla election to Mohanty by 5,205 votes. His election petition had reached the evidence stage, with two witnesses examined, before he sought withdrawal on March 30 following instructions from the partyâs central leadership. Justice Mishra allowed the withdrawal the same day. title: A Kerala passenger received â¹1 less on his cancelled train ticket and sued IRCTC; two years later, the consumer court ordered the railway corporation to pay â¹3,100 in compensation.
text: (Image Credit: Canva) A one-rupee shortfall in a train ticket refund led a passenger from Kerala to take the Indian Railway Catering and Tourism Corporation ( IRCTC ) to the consumer commission. The passenger, who had booked and cancelled a ticket in 2024, won the case, with the Kasaragod District Consumer Commission directing IRCTC to pay â¹3,100 in compensation along with the pending refund amount. However, the refund rules applicable at the time have since been revised. The claimant cancelled his ticket on August 17, 2024, more than 48 hours before the scheduled journey on August 20, 2024. He booked an AC three-tier train ticket for â¹553 on August 11. The complaint mentions that IRCTC deducted â¹180 as cancellation charges and 5 per cent GST, which amounted to â¹9. As calculated, the refund amount came up to â¹341; however, IRCTC refunded only â¹340. This left a shortfall of â¹1. The shortfall caused the complainant confusion and mental distress. This incident caused a breach of trust towards India's primary railway organisation. His demands were â¹1 lakh for confusion, â¹1 lakh for breach of trust, â¹5,000 for litigation costs and the â¹1 shortfall. The commission rejected IRCTC's counter-argument because it was barred by limitation. It was noted that IRCTC did not attempt to justify the â¹1 shortage at the time of the refund. Failing to refund the exact amount was both a deficiency in service and an unfair trade practice. This created a liability for the organisation to refund the deficiency and pay additional compensation. The order by the commission mentioned, "Just because one rupee is paid less, the said fact really counts and the complainant is entitled to Rs 100 as compensation. Complainant is also eligible for the cost of litigation fixed as Rs 3,000." (Image Credit: Wikimedia Commons) The complainant's demands were partly granted. The â¹1 was compensated by paying Rs 100, and additionally, the consumer forum directed IRCTC to pay Rs 3,000 for litigation costs. "...complaint is allowed in part opposite party directed to refund Rs 1 with 9% interest from date of cancellation of date of ticket that is 17.08.2024 till realisation and Rs 100 towards compensation for deficiency in service and unfair trade practices and Rs 3000 as cost of litigation to the complainant within 30 days," the commission, chaired by Krishnan K, ordered. New Cancellation Policy of Indian Railways (Image Credit: Canva) Indian Railways has modified its cancellation and refund policy for confirmed tickets, with the revised rules coming into effect in March 2026. Under the new rules, all cancellation time windows have been increased, giving passengers less flexibility to cancel tickets at the last minute. Earlier, a full refund, after deducting the applicable flat cancellation charge, could be availed if the passenger cancelled tickets more than 48 hours before departure. Now, to get the highest possible refund, tickets must be cancelled more than 72 hours before departure. Thus, the amount refunded to the Kerala passenger would have differed had the new rules applied to his cancellation. Even the 25% and 50% deduction windows have also changed, moving from 48-12 hours to 72-24 hours and from 12-4 hours to 24-8 hours, respectively. Finally, the no-refund window has doubled from the earlier four hours to eight hours. Fully waitlisted e-tickets are automatically cancelled after chart preparation if all passengers remain waitlisted, subject to applicable clerkage deductions. One exception is confirmed Tatkal tickets, which generally receive no refund upon cancellation. However, passengers are eligible for a full refund if the Railways cancels the train. Thus, please plan your journeys ahead of time and avoid any last-minute changes to your plans. Indian Railways' revised policy means passengers may receive a lower refund for modifications made closer to their travel dates. title: Rahul already suffered 56 losses before Gyanendra became CEC, says Patra
text: Sambit Patra in Kashi Varanasi: Escalating the BJP âs counterattack on Rahul Gandhi âs allegations against the Election Commission , party spokesperson Sambit Patra on Monday accused the Congress leader of misleading the nation with claims of the deletion of 13 crore votes. Citing the Congressâs record of repeated electoral defeats, Patra said the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls was a constitutional exercise aimed at updating voter lists, not the âvote theftâ being alleged by the opposition. A day after Gandhiâs mega show at Delhiâs Ramlila Maidan, Patra said the Congress has made it a habit to blame either EVMs or the EC after every electoral defeat. Patra said the BJP had won three Lok Sabha elections in 2014, 2019 and 2024 before Gyanendra Kumar became chief election commissioner on Feb 19, 2025. Referring to Rahulâs allegations against the Election Commission, he said the Congress lost 56 assembly elections between 2014 and 2025, and Rahul should explain those defeats instead of attacking constitutional institutions. He cited the 2014 Lok Sabha election, saying V S Sampath was the CEC then and had been appointed during Congress rule in 2012. âDid Congress appoint him to make Narendra Modi the Prime Minister?â Patra asked, adding that institutions should not be targeted for political convenience. Patra also said the Congress has been out of power for decades in several states, including Tamil Nadu for 59 years, West Bengal for 49 years, Uttar Pradesh for 37 years, Bihar for 36 years, Tripura for 33 years and Odisha for 26 years. He said these defeats were due to the Congressâs political failures, not voter-list revision. Defending the SIR, Patra said it had been conducted 12 times in the country, 10 times under Congress govts and twice under BJP govts. He said names are removed on four grounds, including absent, shifted, deceased and duplicate voters. Rahul Gandhi was combining different categories to falsely allege the theft of 13 crore votes, he added. He said around three crore people were marked absent, six crore applied through Form-6 for inclusion, and notices were issued to six crore shifted voters. Patra also said 2.37 crore young voters aged 18 to 28 had been added since June 2025. Targeting former West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee, Patra said only Indian citizens have the right to vote and infiltrators cannot be allowed into voter lists. He challenged Congress and Samajwadi Party booth agents to identify errors instead of making allegations. title: Dhinidhi Desinghu scripts history with first-ever Indian swimming medal at Youth Olympics
text: Dhinidhi Desinghu (File photo) BENGALURU: Indian swimming has a new milestone to celebrate, and Bengaluru talent Dhinidhi Desinghu is at the heart of it. The 16-year-old became the first swimmer from the country to win a medal at the Youth Olympic Games, claiming bronze in the women's 100m freestyle in Dakar, Senegal, on Monday. While Dhinidhi had set her sights on gold and a sub-55-second finish, her podium finish was a historic achievement for Indian swimming. Croatia's Ana Bobanovic took gold in 55.89 seconds, while New Zealand's Alyssa Lawson claimed silver in 56.13 seconds. The performance had been building momentum from the heats. Dhinidhi clocked 56.80 seconds to finish third-fastest overall and become the first Indian female swimmer to qualify for a Youth Olympics final. She carried that form into the final. âI'm very happy but also at a loss for words. In the heats, my timing went below 57. I've never had a time below 57 in the event, and I knew something special would happen," she told TOI. Going into the final, there was a mix of nerves and confidence. The conditions, too, worked in her favour. "Generally, when I swim outdoors, and it's hot and humid, I swim better, because the conditions are similar to what it is back home," she said. The result, however, was initially not quite what she had hoped for. "When I touched the pad and saw the timing, I wasn't very happy. I wanted to win gold and I wanted my time to break 55, but didnât achieve either. But slowly it sank in â I am India's first swimmer to win a medal at the Youth Olympics and that does mean something special," added the teenager, who trains under Nihar Ameen. The win's significance went beyond the medal itself. Dhinidi believes her podium finish is a breakthrough for women's swimming in the country. "I think what makes it more special is that it's a woman who has given India its first medal in swimming in the competition. It will mean a lot for women's swimming because we're not at the same level as the men. This will make it a memorable chapter in women's swimming in our country and help in the growth of our sport," she said. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines She is the third Indian to reach a final at the competition, after two-time Olympian Srihari Nataraj, who made the final in 2018, and Tirthank Pegu, who is competing in the ongoing edition. But milestones are nothing new to her. Dhinidhi was just 14 when she made her Olympic debut at Paris 2024, becoming the youngest member of the Indian contingent. She had also represented India at the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou and the 2024 World Aquatics Championships in Doha. For now, the triumph is still sinking in. âIt (medal) will take some time to sink in. After Paris, it took a couple of years to sink in that I was an Olympian. So, it is safe to say this will take a long time to sink in," she signed off. Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

title: US midterms 2026: Meet Suhas Subramanyam, Indian-origin Democrat who served as advisor to Barack Obama
text: Suhas Subramanyam of Virginia is among several Indian-origin candidates contesting the US midterm elections on November 3. The Democrat is seeking re-election from Virginiaâs 10th Congressional District, where he faces Republican challenger Dave Beckwith, a 30-year veteran of the US Air Force. A lawyer by profession, Subramanyam served as a White House policy advisor during Barack Obamaâs presidency. Family life Born in Virginia in 1979, Subramanyam is the son of Indian immigrants. His mother, a Bengaluru native, moved to the US to join his father, who grew up in Chennai and Secunderabad, and to pursue higher education. Subramanyam is married to Miranda Pena Subramanyam, and the couple have two daughters. The family lives in Loudoun County, Virginia. Education and pre-political career Subramanyam holds a bachelorâs degree from Tulane University and a Juris Doctor (J.D.) from Northwestern Universityâs Pritzker School of Law. Thereafter, he worked as White House technology policy advisor under Obama. After his stint at the White House, Subramanyam launched a small business in Loudoun County and volunteered as an emergency medical technician (EMT) and firefighter. Political career Subramanyam was first elected to the Virginia House of Delegates, where he served from 2019 to 2023, before joining the Virginia State Senate in 2023, serving until 2024. During his time in the state legislature, he passed legislation aimed at lowering tolls, utility bills and prescription drug costs. He also co-founded a caucus focused on bipartisanship and helped pass bipartisan bills on K-12 education, tax cuts and gun safety. Subramanyam was elected to represent Virginiaâs 10th Congressional District in 2024, succeeding retiring Democratic incumbent Jennifer Wexton. He defeated Republican candidate Mike Clancy, securing 215,131 votes against Clancyâs 196,343. Political position Subramanyam has accused US President Donald Trumpâs Republican administration of driving up costs and undermining healthcare and the federal workforce. He has also continued to raise issues affecting Indian professionals, including lengthy green card backlogs and structural challenges with the H-1B visa programme. After US law enforcement foiled an alleged plot to vandalise a Hindu temple in Illinois earlier this month, Subramanyam called on lawmakers from both parties to condemn what he described as rising anti-Indian hostility, hate speech and discrimination. âEvery American deserves to practice their faith without fear of violence. The details of the plot to carry out a shooting at a Hindu temple in Illinois are deeply concerning. I am grateful for the individuals who notified law enforcement, and everyone whose actions prevented this attack. But we need to act now and address the rise of hate in this country. I will continue fighting to ensure that every community can worship safely,â he said in a statement. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

title: Another 'exploding pager' plot? Israel eyes strike on Tehranâs top military bosses
text: Netanyahu holds up pager at UN, recalls Israelâs Hezbollah attack Israel is considering a covert operation modelled on its 2024 exploding-pager attacks against Hezbollah to target Iran's top military and security leadership, potentially eliminating key commanders and disrupting the country's wartime command structure, amid growing uncertainty over the possibility of renewed US-Israeli strikes against Tehran. "According to a report published by the New York Post, former Mossad deputy head of global operations Oded Ailam said Israel could consider a pager-style operation targeting Iran's military establishment, describing the option as 'fully on the table'." Watch Netanyahu's TIME RUNNING OUT? Arab Parties Signal Major Move To Topple Israeli PM After Deadlock He identified four senior figures as the people exercising real power in Tehran, including Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) chief Ahmad Vahidi, Basij commander Hossein Taeb, armed forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi and security official Mohsen Rezaei. Ailam argued that Iran's military establishment has emerged as the principal centre of power, with the country's political leadership struggling to maintain control over strategic decisions. He suggested that disagreements between military hardliners and political officials have also complicated Tehran's negotiations with Washington. The proposed operation draws parallels with Israel's September 2024 covert campaign against Hezbollah, widely referred to as Operation Grim Beeper, in which thousands of pagers and walkie-talkies used by the Iran-backed militant group exploded across Lebanon in two successive waves. The first wave began on September 17, 2024, when thousands of pagers used by Hezbollah operatives exploded almost simultaneously across Lebanon, particularly in Beirut's southern suburbs, the Bekaa Valley and southern Lebanon. The following day, September 18, a second wave targeted handheld walkie-talkies used by the group, triggering explosions in several locations, including during funerals. The two attacks killed at least 39 people and injured more than 3,400, according to Reuters. According to Reuters, Hezbollah had ordered approximately 5,000 AR-924 pagers, which were allegedly modified before reaching the group. Explosives were concealed inside the devices, allowing Israeli intelligence to turn ordinary communication equipment into remotely activated weapons. In December 2024, two former Israeli intelligence officers, speaking anonymously to CBS News' 60 Minutes, disclosed further details about the operation. They said the planning had begun nearly a decade earlier with booby-trapped walkie-talkies, while the pager component was developed from 2022 onwards. The report comes amid growing indications that Washington and Tel Aviv are preparing for a possible resumption of military operations against Iran after the November 3 US midterm elections. A third American aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, is heading towards the Middle East, where it is expected to join the USS George Washington and USS George HW Bush, already deployed in the region. US President Donald Trump told Kansas City radio station KCMO on Friday that the war was "going to get wrapped up soon", without providing details about how or when the conflict would end, according to the report. Retired US Army General Jack Keane argued that any renewed American and Israeli military campaign should target Iran's military leadership alongside its nuclear programme, domestic energy infrastructure and ballistic missile and drone facilities. title: US midterms 2026: Meet Amish Shah, the doctor seeking a second shot at Congress
text: Amish Shah , an emergency-room physician and former Arizona state legislator, is seeking a seat in the US House of Representatives for a second time, placing health-care costs, household affordability and access to federal benefits at the centre of his campaign. The Democrat is contesting Arizona's 1st Congressional District against Republican Jay Feely, a former NFL kicker and sports broadcaster endorsed by President Donald Trump. The November 3, 2026, election follows Republican incumbent David Schweikert's decision to run for governor instead of seeking re-election. Born and raised in Chicago, Shah is the son of Indian immigrants. He graduated from Northwestern University with degrees in economics and medicine, earned a Master of Public Health from the University of California, Berkeley, and completed emergency-medicine training in New York. He later worked as a physician and medical educator before entering politics. Shah served in the Arizona House of Representatives from 2019 to 2024, winning three consecutive elections. He focused on public health, education, small businesses and public safety. In 2024, he contested the congressional seat but lost to Schweikert in a closely fought election. He secured the Democratic nomination in July 2026 after defeating several challengers, including Marlene GalÃ¡n-Woods, who had received backing from the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee. Shah's campaign promises to lower prescription-drug costs, protect Medicare and Social Security, defend abortion rights and address rising household expenses. He has also highlighted Arizona's water security, criticised Trump's tariffs and pledged to oppose data-centre projects over concerns about their water consumption. title: NDA leaders urge rebels to withdraw from AP local body polls
text: CM Chandrababu Naidu with deputy CM Pawan Kalyan during a joint press meet on Tuesday Vijayawada : The top leadership of the NDA alliance on Tuesday appealed to rebel candidates of the TDP , Jana Sena and BJP to respect the allianceâs seat-sharing arrangement and withdraw from the election fray. They appealed to their respective party workers to work for the victory of officially nominated candidates in the local body elections. Addressing a joint press conference, chief minister N Chandrababu Naidu , deputy chief minister K Pawan Kalyan , and BJP state president P V N Madhav said an elaborate exercise was undertaken to finalise seat-sharing and candidate selection at every level of the local body elections. Naidu said the coalition had carefully balanced alliance compulsions, local realities, social engineering and winnability before finalising candidates. He said the exercise was more complex than the one carried out during the 2024 assembly and Lok Sabha elections since seat-sharing had to be worked out down to the MPTC level. Pawan Kalyan said local body elections posed challenges different from those in general elections, as seat adjustments had to be made for thousands of positions. While acknowledging that several aspirants could not be accommodated despite their work for the parties, he assured them that the alliance leadership would do justice to such leaders and workers in future. The alliance leaders urged cadres to uphold the decisions taken by the three parties and campaign only for candidates officially allotted tickets under the coalition arrangement. Naidu said the alliance had taken decisions after extensive consultations and warned that action would be taken against those working against officially nominated candidates. Seeking public support for the coalition, Naidu said local bodies needed to be strengthened and promised greater financial support and development works if NDA-backed candidates were elected. Turning his attack on the YSRCP and its president, YS Jagan Mohan Reddy , Naidu accused the opposition of attempting to stall local body elections through litigation, violence and misinformation. He alleged that the party had filed dozens of court cases seeking to halt the electoral process and was unwilling to accept democratic outcomes. Describing Jaganâs politics as âhit-and-runâ, Naidu said the YSRCPâs ideology is revolving around âcriminalisation, litigation and fake propagandaâ, whereas the NDA stood for welfare, development, governance and public service. The chief minister also urged the YSRCP leadership to abandon violence and join the democratic mainstream. Drawing parallels with his earlier appeals to extremist groups to join the democratic process, Naidu said the opposition should participate in elections and seek votes from the people rather than resorting to confrontation. Escalating the attack further, Naidu referred to the internal disputes within Jaganâs family. He alleged that the Vivekananda Reddy murder case had created a crisis within the family and said disputes over assets had further deepened those divisions. âJaganâs struggle is for his palaces; our struggle is for the poor,â he said. Pawan Kalyan joined the attack by taking exception to remarks made by Jagan. âIf you show 2.0, we will show 10X,â he said, adding that nobody in the alliance was prepared to be intimidated. He said such language reflected weakness rather than strength and suggested that Jagan should heed Naiduâs advice and rejoin the democratic mainstream. Pawan said direct interaction with people would help the former chief minister understand public sentiment. He reiterated that the alliance would remain united despite the complexities of local body elections and would continue to work together for the stateâs development. BJP state president P V N Madhav appealed to voters to bless NDA candidates and said the coalition was delivering welfare, development and good governance with the support of the Centre under Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The NDA leaders maintained that despite intense competition for tickets, the coalition had made every effort to accommodate deserving aspirants and appealed to dissatisfied leaders to put the allianceâs larger objective ahead of individual aspirations. They urged voters to replicate the support extended to the NDA in the 2024 elections and ensure victory for coalition candidates in the local body polls. title: Low-key campaign, voter apathy, political infighting pull down Visakhapatnam turnout
text: A woman shows her inked-finger after casting vote for GVMC polls in Visakhapatnam on Sunday. Pic-A Sarath Kumar Visakhapatnam : Urban voter apathy was once again evident in the GVMC election held on Sunday. O nly 51.47% of voters in Vizag exercised their franchise, according to official data available till 10 pm , the lowest turnout among the major urban local bodies of Andhra Pradesh that went to polls on Sunday. The slow pace of polling in Vizag was evident right from the morning. Only around 3.34% of voters had cast their votes by 9 am. The turnout rose to 26.5% by 1 pm, six hours after polling began at 7 am. The sluggish response continued through the day, pointing to a lack of enthusiasm among urban voters. Low voter turnout has been a recurring feature of elections to the Vizag municipal body. Of the six elections held before Sundayâs poll, turnout crossed 70% only once, in 1981. In all the other elections, it remained below the 60% mark. Sundayâs election followed the same pattern, with polling settling at around 51.5% . This is even lower than the over 59% recorded in the 2021 GVMC elections and far below the 64-76% turnout recorded across different Assembly segments of the city in the 2024 elections. When TOI visited several polling booths in the East, North and South zones, queues were thin right from the morning. This was in sharp contrast to the scenes witnessed during the 2024 elections. Political enthusiasm was largely missing on the streets, except for some activity around polling booths. Several factors appear to have contributed to the subdued voter response. As TOI reported earlier, campaigning for this municipal election was largely lacklustre in Visakhapatnam. Except for the last two days of campaigning on Oct 29 and 30, there was little visible political activity on the streets. Cyclone Arnab also disrupted normal life, public services and campaigning for nearly three days. Before the cyclone, political parties were grappling with internal issues over ticket allotments and rebel candidates. It took nearly a week for the parties to persuade disgruntled aspirants to withdraw from the contest. Even after these efforts, nearly 40 rebel candidates remained in the fray, affecting the election campaign in several wards. The limited campaigning, internal differences within political parties, and disruption caused by the cyclone appear to have together affected voter participation. The late release of manifestos by the main parties may have also contributed to the lack of public engagement. The TDP released its manifesto only on Oct 29, while the YSRCP announced its promises on Oct 30, leaving voters little time to assess their proposals for the city. Another possible factor is the perception among residents that the state and central govts play a bigger role in shaping major projects, infrastructure and policies for Visakhapatnam than the municipal corporation. This could have reduced the importance attached to the local body election by some sections of the electorate. A section of the cityâs educated and working population may also have limited direct engagement with local corporators and mayoral candidates. The presence of several migrant families, some of whom may not have strong connections with local political leaders, could be another factor behind the subdued participation. Speaking to TOI, M Ravi Kanth, who voted at a booth set up at Girijan Bhavan in MVP Colony, said the turnout appeared to be thin. âI came early, thinking I could finish voting before the queues became longer. However, I was surprised to find only a few people waiting. The manifestos and campaigning may not have reached the public. Even from my conversations with friends, the enthusiasm I noticed during the 2024 polls was largely missing this time,â said Ravi Kanth, a private employee. R Srinath, a young voter who was spotted at a polling booth in Peda Waltair, said the political parties had not made any significant announcements for the GVMC elections. âIt has been a complete dud, both in terms of campaigning and election promises,â he said. Apart from minor clashes in a few wards between workers of NDA parties and the YSRCP, polling passed off largely peacefully in Visakhapatnam. The YSRCP, however, alleged rigging in some wards. title: Modi, Shah to spearhead BJPâs campaign for UP polls
text: Union home minister Amit Shah Prime Minister Narendra Modi Union home minister Amit Shah Prime Minister Narendra Modi Union home minister Amit Shah 1 2 Lucknow: BJP is preparing to shift its UP campaign into high gear, with PM Narendra Modi , Union home minister Amit Shah and party national president Nitin Nabin set to spearhead a series of high-profile engagements over a period of one month, signalling the beginning of partyâs intensified organisational and political combat ahead of 2027 elections. The first signs of this mobilisation will be visible on Sunday, when Modi visits his constituency Varanasi to attend the concluding display of the Indian Air Forceâs air show, Wings Over Ganga, at NaMo Ghat. The PM is also scheduled to visit Mirzamurad to inaugurate a new industrial unit of Arvind Mills, projected to generate around 1,000 direct jobs. Watch PM Modi Watches IAF Air Show In Varanasi, Inaugurates Garment Unit Amid Border Row Although no political rally is on Modiâs itinerary, BJP is expected to make the most of his visit to showcase its political strength in his parliamentary constituency. The high-profile engagements come as the party begins groundwork for a state-wide campaign, with organisational consolidation and the revival of its electoral machinery emerging as immediate priorities. From Varanasi, the spotlight is expected to shift to BJPâs much-awaited state executive meeting, where Amit Shah is likely to take stock of the organisation and outline partyâs roadmap for 2027 state polls. Party sources said Shahâs proposed participation in the meeting assumes particular significance even as the BJP seeks to recalibrate its strategy after its unexpected poor performance in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections in UP against the Samajwadi Party. The party has since been reviewing its electoral setbacks, examining district- and constituency-level performance and identifying organisational gaps that may have cost it crucial seats. Shah, widely credited with orchestrating the BJPâs sweeping victory in the 2017 UP elections, is expected to push for a high-intensity, micro-targeted campaign that combines booth-level mobilisation with sharper social and caste outreach. The challenge before the BJP is to recover lost ground while countering an emboldened opposition led by the SP and its ally Congress. The partyâs next phase of preparations is therefore expected to focus not merely on energising its cadre but also on tightening coordination between its organisational leadership, govt and alliance partners. With Modi and Shah expected to anchor the initial phase of the campaign, BJP is also preparing to put the strength of the National Democratic Alliance on public display. A key event in this strategy is a proposed joint rally with ally Om Prakash Rajbharâs Suheldev Bhartiya Samaj Party (SBSP) in Azamgarh on Nov 29. Tentatively billed as the Samajik Samrasta Maharally, the event is expected to be attended by Nitin Nabin, Yogi Adityanath and UP BJP president Pankaj Chaudhary. Other NDA partners, including Apna Dal (S), the Nishad Party and the Rashtriya Lok Dal, are also expected to participate. SBSP national general secretary Arun Rajbhar confirmed that the rally would be a âshow of strengthâ by the BJP-led NDA in eastern Uttar Pradesh or Purvanchal. The choice of Azamgarh is politically significant. Regarded as an SP bastion, the district presents the BJP-led alliance with an opportunity to challenge the opposition on its home turf and demonstrate that its social coalition remains intact ahead of the Assembly polls. In the 2022 Assembly elections, SP won all 10 seats in Azamgarh district. The party subsequently won the Azamgarh Lok Sabha seat in 2024 Lok Sabha elections with SPâs Dharmendra Yadav defeating BJP candidate Dinesh Lal Yadav âNirahuaâ by more than 1.6 lakh votes. The proposed rally is thus being positioned as more than a show of alliance unity. It is also expected to serve as a platform for consolidating the BJPâs outreach among OBCs, particularly the Most Backward Classes (MBCs), whose electoral support could prove crucial in the closely contested political battle ahead. title: Boxing Federation of India mess: Ajay Singh's rival faction meets Raksha Khadse, IOA CEO; alleges support of 27 units
text: Boxing Federation of India (BFI) members discussed their way forward against current president Ajay Singh in a meeting in New Delhi. (Photo by special arrangement) NEW DELHI: Amid an ongoing political tussle, the Boxing Federation of India's (BFI) affiliaited units and executive committee (ExCo) members sat in one room on Wednesday in New Delhi to showcase their unity and strength against the current president, Ajay Singh . Claiming the support of 27 out of 35 units and 8 of 13 ExCo members, the faction met Minister of State for Youth Affairs & Sports Raksha Khadse and Indian Olympic Association (IOA) CEO Raghuram Iyer to register their concerns via a memorandum. It was originally scheduled to be a Special General Meeting (SGM) and vote of no-confidence against Singh. Those plans were shelved by the Punjab and Haryana High Court, which put the SGM in abeyance until November 13. Watch Bombay Sport Exchange: Mustafa Ghouse on ISL, India's sporting ecosystem and grassroots problem That, however, didn't dissuade the hierarchy from coming together and expressing their displeasure with the three-time BFI president and his tenure. BFI secretary general Pramod Kumar - who was suspended by Singh - treasurer Pon Baskaran, vice-president Rajesh Bhandari, Delhi Amateur Boxing Association vice-president Rohit Jain and others said they submitted a memorandum to the Sports Ministry, the IOA and World Boxing president Gennadiy Golovkin. The memorandum accused Singh of concentrating powers in his hands, sidelining elected office-bearers and undermining democratic processes within the federation. Separately, the group alleged administrative lapses, disregard for the constitution and a âHitler-ish approachâ by Singh. "We have given our memorandum to them (Sports Ministry). Whatever issued we have, whether it is related to the constitution or technical conduct, whether it is related to coaching or selection committee, and about the administration, we have told him everything. Now, it is his decision. And we have also written to the global body. Unfortunately, the meeting we wanted to hold today wasn't possible, but let's see what changes from here," said Bhandari. "Every time an official within the Boxing Federation has questioned Ajay Singh's authority, they have either been suspended or served with a show-cause notice. If we do not get any respite from this situation, it is possible that we will sit at Jantar Mantar in the coming days," said BFI Senior VP Rajesh Bhandari. Left to right: BFI Vice President Rajesh Bhandari, Secretary General Pramod Kumar and VP of Delhi Amateur Boxing Association Rohit Jain. (Photo by special arrangement) Rohit Jain, who has challenged Singh's presidency in the past and vows to do so again, claimed the biggest issue is the constitutional overreach. "This battle started in 2024. They modified the constitution as such that it suits them. They rested all the powers at the seat of the president. They suspend any state unit without giving a notice, without assigning any reasons. Have you ever heard that someone will be suspended without giving a reason and an ad-hoc committee be formed? The main reason for this, I have to say, is that I have experienced the pain. They wanted to keep me away from boxing and competition so that I could not win the elections and could not stand in front of them. They changed the constitution not once, but twice," he said. BFI claims support of 21 authorised units On the same day, 21 of BFI's 35 authorised state units participated in a two-day âMission Olympic Podiumâ meeting in Bagdogra. Representatives of 18 units attended in person, while three joined through video conferencing. The participating units included the ad hoc committees of Mizoram and Jharkhand along with the BFI Athletes committee player representative. âOur responsibility is to the boxers and their future. The participation of a majority of our authorised state units demonstrates their commitment to working together as a federation towards our Olympic ambitions, with athletes at the centre of that effort. The work begins in the states â identifying talent, supporting coaches and creating a clear pathway for boxers to progress, gain competitive exposure and represent India. The latest developments come as the administrative chaos in the BFI continues for a third year running. The current logjam was heightened after Ajay Singh suspended Pramod Kumar, who had challenged the presidentâs authority. Singh has argued that his removal will require support from three-fourths of the General Body members. But for that, SGM needs to be called as per the constitutional norms. title: Blue wave meets red flag: On cusp of big win, Democrats face internal sabotage
text: Rep. Haley Stevens (AP Photo) TOI Correspondent From Washington: Just when Democrats in America were beginning to entertain thoughts of a blue wave, possibly even a blue tsunami, along came Haley Stevens to remind them that nobody is quite as capable of complicating Democratic fortunes as a Democrat. In an extraordinary convulsion barely 48 hours before Tuesday's midterm elections, the Democratic Michigan congresswoman, who lost a bitter party primary (inner party election) to progressive Abdul El-Sayed, crossed the political aisle to endorse his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, in what would be called a last minute âdefectionâ in Indian political parlance. The immediate political damage is difficult to quantify, but the optics and the timing â coming just when many polls are showing a Republican rout â could hardly be worse for Democrats, who are trying to persuade voters that they are united and ready to take back control of Washington. Instead, one of their own has provided Republicans with a ready-made advertisement for Democratic disarray. MAGA boss Donald Trump immediately jumped on the break, praising her âbravery. â The Stevens-El-Sayed rupture had been simmering since a bitter August primary,, which El-Sayed won by less than one percent. It was not simply a case of a disappointed politician nursing wounded ambitions within the party; the two represent sharply different constituencies and political instincts, particularly over Israel and the Gaza war. Stevens, a staunch supporter of Israel, was bankrolled by the so-called âJewish lobby.â El-Sayed, a progressive son of Egyptian immigrants, campaigned on a more critical position towards Israeli policy and US military support for Israel. The primary exposed fault lines between pro-Israel Dems and the party's vocal progressive wing, and the schism is now threatening to play out nationally, undercutting polls pointing to a big win. Stevens initially endorsed El-Sayed after losing -- albeit without much enthusiasm -- but the truce was always more a marriage of political convenience than a true reconciliation. The trigger for the final explosion was an ad by El-Sayed supporters linking U.S financial support for Israel to the rising cost of groceries. Stevens considered the advertisement antisemitic and demanded that El-Sayed disavow it. He eventually rejected the ad's contents, but the dispute had gone personal by then, with El Sayed, likely emboldened by polls showing he was leading by 10+ points, torching a planned joint church appearance with Stevens and asking her to take a walk. She walked -- over to Republican candidate Mike Rogers. Such election-eve defections being rare in America, Democratic leaders were aghast, even as Trump and his flock welcomed her. Democratic Party boss and NY Senator Chuck Schumer, who had backed Stevens during the primary, called her decision a "despicable betrayal," while furious party flacks like James Carville used gross reproductive metaphors to warn her that Republicans would use her and discard. Democratic partisans are still hoping that a NYT/Siena poll showing the party leading in all seven crucial Senate -- five of them by +5 percent â--can withstand the last minute Stephens torpedo. The numbers are unbelievable for Dems, particularly in Kansas and Texas, where they have not won a Senate seat in decades. Even allowing for polling error, the geographical breadth of the Democratic advantage suggests a national political environment hostile to Republicans. Still, the Dem are nervous, and the feeling is not entirely irrational. The party has repeatedly discovered that the electorate it sees in surveys is not necessarily the one that turns up at polling stations. Donald Trump's political career has been built, in considerable measure, on voters who are difficult for traditional polling models to capture: less politically engaged people, rural and small-town voters, working-class whites, and those who are reluctant to identify openly with MAGA and some of its nativist and racist agenda. The 2016 election remains the defining example. Hillary Clinton's 97 percent winning certainty evaporated in the industrial Midwest and boondocks America, where Trump mobilised voters who had been insufficiently represented in polling samples and turnout assumptions. Even in 2024, Dems were surprised by the extent of Trump's support among working-class voters, including sections of the electorate that had previously been part of their coalition. This is the so-called hidden Trump voter: somebody who may not be particularly enthusiastic about the Republican Party, may not even like Trump personally, but will turn up to vote Republican when sufficiently motivated. There is another complication: Midterm elections generally have a different electorate from presidential contests. Older, more habitual voters tend to dominate, while younger and less politically engaged voters are more likely to stay home. That will favour Republicans if the Democratic advantage in current surveys â captured by a range of pollsters from Nate Silver to NYT, from Emerson College to Marist University â does not translate into actual turnout. Republicans, meanwhile, have their own problems. Trump's economic message of unprecedented prosperity is difficult to reconcile with voters worried about grocery bills, tariffs and household expenses. His rallies, which many now see as entertainment, may fill arenas but they do not necessarily fill ballot boxes. The most important question on Tuesday will therefore not be whether Democrats are ahead in the polls, which they are. It will be whether their lead survives the transition from the pollster's carefully constructed likely-voter sample to the rather less predictable business of actually voting. You use AI every day.
